tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

## Notes/Tips from Spec
Mutation 3 asks for a tree of a million
nodes, and valgrind runs many times slower than native. Put the million-node case behind a flag
or its own target so make memcheck still finishes inside a coffee break: run the large case under
asan, which is fast enough, and a smaller case under valgrind. What you must not do is quietly
shrink the large case because a timing problem was inconvenient. If your harness ends up running
the “million-node” teardown at ten thousand nodes, say so in REFLECTION.md, and expect the
walkthrough to ask about it.

CC := gcc
CFLAGS := -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Iinclude
# TEST_CFLAGS is recursively expanded (=, not :=) so it picks up the
# asan target's target-specific `CFLAGS +=` override at build time.
TEST_CFLAGS = $(CFLAGS) -DRBTREE_TEST_HOOKS
SRC := src/rbtree.c
TSRC := tests/test_rbtree.c
BIN := build/test_rbtree
FUZZBIN := build/fuzz

all: $(BIN) $(FUZZBIN)

$(BIN): $(SRC) $(TSRC) include/rbtree.h
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CC) $(TEST_CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC) -o $@

$(FUZZBIN): $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c include/rbtree.h
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c -o $@

test: $(BIN) $(FUZZBIN)
	./$(BIN) && ./$(FUZZBIN) 100000

asan: CFLAGS += -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer
asan: clean test

memcheck: all
	valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all \
		--error-exitcode=1 ./$(BIN)
	valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all \
		--error-exitcode=1 ./$(FUZZBIN) 20000
clean:
	rm -rf build

.PHONY: all test asan memcheck clean

# Mutation 1 — allocation-failure fault injection: analysis & plan

## Context

HW2 requires every heap allocation in `src/rbtree.c` to be checked, with every failure
leaving the tree byte-for-byte unchanged, caller-owned values still caller-owned, and no
leaks (`make asan` / `make memcheck` clean). Today `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are `static`
pass-throughs to libc, and `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` are empty stubs. Mutation 1 is the
work that turns the seam into something a deterministic fault injector can sit underneath,
and proves `rb_insert` (the only non-trivial allocator in the file) is atomic against
injected failures. This plan is built from the actual current `src/rbtree.c` /
`include/rbtree.h` / `tests/test_rbtree.c` and from CLAUDE.md/NOTES.md — I could not read
`CS370-HW2.pdf` directly (no `pdftotext`/`poppler-utils` in this environment), so anything
here that assumes Mutation 1's scope boundary should be checked against the PDF's own
wording before final sign-off.

## 1. Every allocation reachable from `rb_insert`, in source order

`rb_insert` (`src/rbtree.c:120-158`):

| # | Line | Allocation | Owner immediately after success | On failure | Resource(s) to release |
|---|------|------------|----------------------------------|------------|-------------------------|
| — | 126-129 (overwrite, `cmp==0`) | **none** | n/a | n/a (cannot fail) | n/a |
| 1 | 135 `n = rb_malloc(sizeof *n)` | new node struct | local `n` (not yet linked into the tree) | `return -1` immediately (136) | nothing — this was the only thing acquired, and it never succeeded |
| 2 | 139 `n->key = rb_malloc(keylen)` | key copy | local `n->key` (still not linked into the tree) | `rb_free(n); return -1;` (140-142) | `n` (the node struct from #1) |

No other `rb_malloc` call exists anywhere in `rb_insert`. `rb_create` (line 30-37) has
exactly one more allocation in the whole file (the `rbtree_t` struct itself), fails with
`return NULL` before any state exists, and already needs no unwind.

## 2. Candidate commit point

Line 151-153:
```c
if (parent == NULL)      t->root = n;
else if (cmp < 0)        parent->left = n;
else                     parent->right = n;
```
This is the **first** line that mutates the tree itself (first write to `t->root` or to an
existing node's `left`/`right`). Everything before it — both `rb_malloc` calls, `memcpy`,
and populating `n`'s fields — touches only the new, not-yet-linked node.

## 3. Failure points vs. the commit point

Both allocation failure points (#1 and #2 above) occur **strictly before** line 151 — by
construction, since both `rb_malloc` calls happen textually earlier and nothing branches
back. Consequence: **`insert_fixup` can never run on a failed `rb_insert`** — it is only
called (line 155) after the unconditional link-in, so there is no fixup-reachable fault
path to worry about at all for Mutation 1. There are no failure points after the commit
point in the current code, and none should be introduced.

## 4. Error-path structure

**No new structure is needed.** The acquire-everything-before-mutating-anything ordering
already gives failure atomicity for free: at every failure point there is at most one
resource to release (none for #1, just `n` for #2), and the existing plain
`if (... == NULL) { cleanup; return -1; }` pairs already do that, LIFO, with no reordering
required. Per CLAUDE.md ("do not add cleanup paths that can instead be designed away") and
the house goto-cleanup rule (reserved for *multi-step* unwinds), introducing a
`goto cleanup` label here would be unneeded ceremony for a single-step release — recommend
leaving this exactly as-is. Flagging this as a judgment call since you said you'd push
back: if the grading rubric wants goto-cleanup unconditionally for any function with ≥2
allocations regardless of unwind complexity, that's a style call to settle explicitly.

## 5. Overwrite-existing-key path (lines 126-129)

- **Allocates today?** No — `cmp == 0` returns before either `rb_malloc` call.
- **Needs to allocate?** No — the key already matches via `strcmp`, so no new key copy or
  node is ever needed.
- **Old value ownership:** the tree already owns it (absorbed on a prior successful
  insert); `t->value_free(cur->value)` (line 127) is the tree releasing its own property,
  matching the header's "sole owner at that instant" contract.
- **New value ownership transfer:** immediate and unconditional at line 128
  (`cur->value = value`) — since this path cannot fail, there is no partial-ownership
  window to protect. This means the overwrite path has **zero allocation-failure modes**
  under Mutation 1; the fault injector should have nothing to inject here, and a test
  should affirmatively prove that (section 8, item 4).

## 6. `rb_delete` allocation surface

Full read of `rb_delete`/`transplant`/`delete_fixup` (lines 188-284): no call to
`rb_malloc` anywhere — only `rb_free` (lines 255, 278, 281). `rb_delete` must gain no new
allocation-failure mode in Mutation 1, and today it has none to begin with. A fault
injector set to fail on the very next allocation should still let `rb_delete` succeed,
since it never asks the allocator for anything (test in section 8, item 6).

## 7. Fault-sweep harness design

**The one necessary `src/rbtree.c` touch.** `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are currently `static`,
so nothing outside the translation unit can override them — `tests/fault_alloc.c` cannot
intercept calls as the file is structured today. Minimal fix: wrap the two definitions in
`#ifndef RBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC` and drop `static`, so:
- normal builds (`test`, `asan`, `memcheck`'s `test_rbtree`/`fuzz` binaries): unchanged,
  `rbtree.c` defines them itself, pass through to libc.
- a new fault-sweep binary compiles `rbtree.c -DRBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC`, so `rbtree.c` only
  *declares* (not defines) `rb_malloc`/`rb_free`, and links `tests/fault_alloc.c`'s
  definitions instead.

This is a mechanical linkage change only — no logic in `rb_insert`/`rb_delete` changes.

**`tests/fault_alloc.c` injector:**
- global call counter + `fail_at` threshold (0/`SIZE_MAX` sentinel = never fail).
- `rb_malloc`: increment counter; if counter == `fail_at`, return `NULL` without touching
  libc; else forward to real `malloc`.
- `rb_free`: always forwards to real `free` (never injected — the spec's failure modes are
  about allocation, not deallocation).
- `fault_alloc_reset()` / `fault_alloc_set_fail_at(n)` to re-arm between sweep iterations.

**Deterministic fixed scenario:** a small, hand-picked, non-random sequence of `rb_insert`
calls (reused identically every iteration) chosen to at least trigger one rotation/recolor
in `insert_fixup`, so the sweep also demonstrates failures never reach fixup (section 3),
not just that the two `if`-checks exist. No randomness — every iteration's failing call
must be exactly reproducible and nameable in a failure report.

**Loop over n / termination:** run the scenario once with the injector disabled to learn
`N` = total `rb_malloc` calls the scenario makes end-to-end. Then for `fail_at` in `1..N`:
reset injector, arm `fail_at`, rebuild a fresh tree, replay the full scenario. The loop
ends when `fail_at > N` — every allocation call site in the scenario has been exercised
exactly once. This is exhaustive, not a guessed iteration count.

**`assert_unchanged` helper:** before the scenario reaches the call site that will be made
to fail, snapshot `rb_size(t)` plus the full in-order key/value sequence (via `rb_foreach`
into a local array — same tool `test_rbtree.c` already has available). After the induced
`-1` return, re-snapshot and assert both are identical, plus `rb_validate(t) == 0` still
holds.

**Counting destructor for ownership:** reuse the existing `counting_free`/`free_count`
pattern already in `tests/test_rbtree.c` (lines 69-94 — `free_count` incremented by a
`value_free` passed to `rb_create`). After an induced failure on `rb_insert(t, key, &v)`,
assert `free_count` did **not** increase for `v` (tree never absorbed it) and that the
test can safely treat `v` as still its own (no double-free under asan if the test frees
it itself afterward).

**Checked after every injected failure:**
1. return code is exactly `-1`.
2. `assert_unchanged` (size + contents + `rb_validate == 0`).
3. zero leaks — the whole sweep binary runs under `make asan`/`make memcheck` like any
   other target, so the half-built node/key from section 1 must not leak.
4. the counting destructor shows the passed-in value untouched (caller still owns it).
5. tree remains fully usable afterward (can still insert/delete/validate other keys),
   confirming the failure didn't leave stale structure even though nothing was linked in.

## 8. Tests to write first, before touching `rbtree.c`

1. `tests/fault_alloc.c`/`.h` itself (the injector) — infrastructure, no tree logic.
2. Fail allocation **#1** (node struct) on an empty tree: assert `-1`, `rb_size==0`,
   `rb_find` absent, `rb_validate==0`, value not freed.
3. Fail allocation **#2** (key copy): same assertions, plus confirms `n` from #1 was
   actually released (covered by asan/valgrind on this test, not a manual check).
4. Overwrite-path test: arm `fail_at=1` on a tree that already has the key, call
   `rb_insert` again with the same key — must still **succeed** (proves section 5: no
   allocation occurs on overwrite at all).
5. `rb_create` failure test: fail its one malloc, assert `NULL` returned.
6. `rb_delete`-makes-no-allocation test: arm `fail_at=1` (fail the very next allocation),
   call `rb_delete` on an existing tree, assert it still returns `0` and removes correctly.
7. The full deterministic fault-sweep (section 7) over `fail_at = 1..N`, each iteration
   asserting the section-7 checklist.
8. Only after 1-7 pass against the **current** `rbtree.c` should the seam-linkage change
   (dropping `static`, `#ifndef RBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC`) be made — and per section 1/4, no
   `rb_insert`/`rb_delete` logic change is anticipated, only that linkage edit plus a new
   Makefile target to build/run the fault-sweep binary.

## 9. Risks / assumptions

- Could not read `CS370-HW2.pdf` directly in this environment (no poppler-utils) to
  confirm Mutation 1's scope boundary in the spec's own words — this plan is built from
  CLAUDE.md + NOTES.md + the actual code. Worth a manual cross-check before treating this
  as final.
- The `static` → `#ifndef`-guarded linkage change is a real (if small) edit to
  `src/rbtree.c`, not purely test-side — flagging since "Mutation 1" might have been
  framed as test-only work.
- One-induced-failure-per-iteration design doesn't test a *second* failure later in the
  same tree's life after an earlier successful retry — likely out of scope per "every
  allocation may fail" being evaluated independently, but worth confirming against the
  spec rather than assuming.
- `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` symbol ownership will need a settled convention before Mutation 2
  (`src/pool.c`'s slab allocator) also wants to sit under the same seam — likely via
  separate build targets/macros rather than runtime dispatch, but not this mutation's
  problem to solve now; flagging so it isn't rediscovered as a surprise later.

entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

I re-read the actual files. One correction to flag before the redesign: the current `Makefile` does **not** link `tests/fault_alloc.c` into either binary today (`$(BIN)` = `src/rbtree.c tests/test_rbtree.c`, `$(FUZZBIN)` = `src/rbtree.c tests/fuzz.c`), and both `tests/fault_alloc.c` and `tests/fault_alloc.h` are currently 0 bytes. So "already links it" describes the target wiring this mutation needs to add, not current state — worth confirming that's what you meant, since it changes what counts as in-scope for this step (Makefile edit + fault_alloc.{c,h} content, vs. just fault_alloc.{c,h} content).

**What was wrong in my original plan:**
- Invented `fault_alloc_reset()`/`fault_alloc_set_fail_at()` instead of using the required `fault_alloc_arm(long n)` / `fault_alloc_disarm()` / `fault_alloc_total()`.
- Proposed a `#ifndef RBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC`-guarded dual definition of `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` plus a separate macro-built "sweep binary." Unnecessary: if `tests/fault_alloc.c` is linked into *every* test binary and just passes through to real `malloc`/`free` while disarmed, there's no need for two build configurations at all — one binary, always capable of fault injection, inert unless armed.
- Proposed a dry-run-first sweep (compute `N`, then loop `1..N`). The actual termination rule is simpler: increment `n`, rerun the fixed scenario each time, stop the first time a run completes without the armed failure ever triggering.
- Didn't distinguish a failure landing in `rb_create`'s allocation from one landing in a later `rb_insert`'s — these need different assertions.

**Revised seam design (section 7):**
- `src/rbtree.c:24-25` loses its two `static` definitions of `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` entirely — it keeps only plain (non-static) prototypes for them, defined nowhere in `rbtree.c`.
- `tests/fault_alloc.c` becomes the **sole** definition site, in every build: `rb_malloc` increments an internal call counter; while disarmed it just forwards to `malloc`; while armed, if this call is the n-th since `fault_alloc_arm(n)`, return `NULL` without calling `malloc`. `rb_free` always forwards to `free` unconditionally (deallocation is never injected). `fault_alloc_arm(n)` sets the target and resets the counter to 0; `fault_alloc_disarm()` turns injection off (pure pass-through, counter still advances for `fault_alloc_total()`'s benefit); `fault_alloc_total()` returns calls-since-last-arm.
- `Makefile` needs `tests/fault_alloc.c` added as a source to both `$(BIN)` and `$(FUZZBIN)` rules (the only build-file change) — no new macro, no new target.
- No macro conditional, no separate sweep binary: a single build where fault injection is always linked but a no-op until armed.

**Revised sweep termination (section 7):**
```
n = 1
loop:
    fault_alloc_arm(n)
    t = rb_create(counting_free)
    if (t == NULL):
        assert fault_alloc_total() == n      # rb_create's own malloc was the n-th call
        n++; continue
    for (key, value) in fixed_scenario:
        snapshot = capture(t)                 # size + in-order contents, pre-call
        rc = rb_insert(t, key, value)
        if (rc == -1):
            assert_unchanged(t, snapshot)       # identical to state just before this call
            assert value not absorbed (counting destructor unchanged)
            assert fault_alloc_total() == n
            goto end_of_iteration
    if loop reached end of fixed_scenario with no -1:
        rb_destroy(t); fault_alloc_disarm(); break   # fault never reached -> sweep done
    rb_destroy(t); fault_alloc_disarm()
    n++
```
No preliminary dry run to learn `N` — the natural stopping condition (a full scenario replay completes with no induced failure) *is* the termination rule, exactly as specified.

**Revised ordered test plan (section 8):**
1. `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` implementing exactly `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`, `fault_alloc_arm(long)`, `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)`, plus the `Makefile` edit adding it to both binaries' sources.
2. A disarmed-mode sanity test: with the injector linked but never armed, the existing `test_rbtree`/`fuzz` suites still pass unchanged (proves pass-through behavior is truly transparent).
3. `fault_alloc_arm(1)` immediately before `rb_create` on a fresh program: assert `rb_create` returns `NULL`, `fault_alloc_total()==1`.
4. `fault_alloc_arm(2)` with `rb_create` succeeding (its 1 alloc) and the fixed scenario's first `rb_insert` node-struct alloc as call 2: assert `-1`, `assert_unchanged`, value not absorbed.
5. `fault_alloc_arm(3)` landing on that same insert's key-copy alloc: same assertions, and this pair (4 vs 5) should be externally indistinguishable except for which internal alloc failed.
6. Overwrite-path test: arm the very next call, then overwrite an existing key — must still succeed (section 5's "overwrite never allocates" claim, now checkable with the real interface).
7. `rb_delete`-allocates-nothing test: arm the very next call, call `rb_delete` on an existing tree, assert it still returns `0`.
8. The full sweep loop above, run to its natural termination, under both `make asan` and `make memcheck`.

I'll update sections 7 and 8 of the plan file with this now — want me to proceed, or do you want to adjust anything first (e.g. the exact fields `assert_unchanged`/`capture` compare, or whether `fault_alloc_total()` should count only while armed vs. always)?

## 7. Fault-sweep harness design

**The one necessary `src/rbtree.c` touch.** `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are currently `static`,
so nothing outside the translation unit can override them — `tests/fault_alloc.c` cannot
intercept calls as the file is structured today. Minimal fix: wrap the two definitions in
`#ifndef RBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC` and drop `static`, so:
- normal builds (`test`, `asan`, `memcheck`'s `test_rbtree`/`fuzz` binaries): unchanged,
  `rbtree.c` defines them itself, pass through to libc.
- a new fault-sweep binary compiles `rbtree.c -DRBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC`, so `rbtree.c` only
  *declares* (not defines) `rb_malloc`/`rb_free`, and links `tests/fault_alloc.c`'s
  definitions instead.

This is a mechanical linkage change only — no logic in `rb_insert`/`rb_delete` changes.

**`tests/fault_alloc.c` injector:**
- global call counter + `fail_at` threshold (0/`SIZE_MAX` sentinel = never fail).
- `rb_malloc`: increment counter; if counter == `fail_at`, return `NULL` without touching
  libc; else forward to real `malloc`.
- `rb_free`: always forwards to real `free` (never injected — the spec's failure modes are
  about allocation, not deallocation).
- `fault_alloc_reset()` / `fault_alloc_set_fail_at(n)` to re-arm between sweep iterations.

**Deterministic fixed scenario:** a small, hand-picked, non-random sequence of `rb_insert`
calls (reused identically every iteration) chosen to at least trigger one rotation/recolor
in `insert_fixup`, so the sweep also demonstrates failures never reach fixup (section 3),
not just that the two `if`-checks exist. No randomness — every iteration's failing call
must be exactly reproducible and nameable in a failure report.

**Loop over n / termination:** run the scenario once with the injector disabled to learn
`N` = total `rb_malloc` calls the scenario makes end-to-end. Then for `fail_at` in `1..N`:
reset injector, arm `fail_at`, rebuild a fresh tree, replay the full scenario. The loop
ends when `fail_at > N` — every allocation call site in the scenario has been exercised
exactly once. This is exhaustive, not a guessed iteration count.

**`assert_unchanged` helper:** before the scenario reaches the call site that will be made
to fail, snapshot `rb_size(t)` plus the full in-order key/value sequence (via `rb_foreach`
into a local array — same tool `test_rbtree.c` already has available). After the induced
`-1` return, re-snapshot and assert both are identical, plus `rb_validate(t) == 0` still
holds.

**Counting destructor for ownership:** reuse the existing `counting_free`/`free_count`
pattern already in `tests/test_rbtree.c` (lines 69-94 — `free_count` incremented by a
`value_free` passed to `rb_create`). After an induced failure on `rb_insert(t, key, &v)`,
assert `free_count` did **not** increase for `v` (tree never absorbed it) and that the
test can safely treat `v` as still its own (no double-free under asan if the test frees
it itself afterward).

**Checked after every injected failure:**
1. return code is exactly `-1`.
2. `assert_unchanged` (size + contents + `rb_validate == 0`).
3. zero leaks — the whole sweep binary runs under `make asan`/`make memcheck` like any
   other target, so the half-built node/key from section 1 must not leak.
4. the counting destructor shows the passed-in value untouched (caller still owns it).
5. tree remains fully usable afterward (can still insert/delete/validate other keys),
   confirming the failure didn't leave stale structure even though nothing was linked in.

## 8. Tests to write first, before touching `rbtree.c`

1. `tests/fault_alloc.c`/`.h` itself (the injector) — infrastructure, no tree logic.
2. Fail allocation **#1** (node struct) on an empty tree: assert `-1`, `rb_size==0`,
   `rb_find` absent, `rb_validate==0`, value not freed.
3. Fail allocation **#2** (key copy): same assertions, plus confirms `n` from #1 was
   actually released (covered by asan/valgrind on this test, not a manual check).
4. Overwrite-path test: arm `fail_at=1` on a tree that already has the key, call
   `rb_insert` again with the same key — must still **succeed** (proves section 5: no
   allocation occurs on overwrite at all).
5. `rb_create` failure test: fail its one malloc, assert `NULL` returned.
6. `rb_delete`-makes-no-allocation test: arm `fail_at=1` (fail the very next allocation),
   call `rb_delete` on an existing tree, assert it still returns `0` and removes correctly.
7. The full deterministic fault-sweep (section 7) over `fail_at = 1..N`, each iteration
   asserting the section-7 checklist.
8. Only after 1-7 pass against the **current** `rbtree.c` should the seam-linkage change
   (dropping `static`, `#ifndef RBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC`) be made — and per section 1/4, no
   `rb_insert`/`rb_delete` logic change is anticipated, only that linkage edit plus a new
   Makefile target to build/run the fault-sweep binary.

## 7. Fault-sweep harness design

### 7a. Seam linkage — exact definition site per Makefile target

Current `Makefile` link lines (confirmed by re-reading it, not the HW2 starter — see the
note at the top of this plan: no separate starter Makefile file exists in this repo and I
have no PDF-text access to CS370-HW2.pdf in this environment, so this trace is against the
actual current `Makefile` only):

```
$(BIN):     $(CC) $(TEST_CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC)         -o $@   # src/rbtree.c + tests/test_rbtree.c
$(FUZZBIN): $(CC) $(CFLAGS)      $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c    -o $@   # src/rbtree.c + tests/fuzz.c
```

Neither currently lists `tests/fault_alloc.c`. Required edit: add `tests/fault_alloc.c` to
*both* link lines (and as a prerequisite, alongside `tests/fault_alloc.h`, so touching the
injector triggers a rebuild):

```
$(BIN):     $(SRC) $(TSRC) tests/fault_alloc.c tests/fault_alloc.h include/rbtree.h
	$(CC) $(TEST_CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC) tests/fault_alloc.c -o $@

$(FUZZBIN): $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c tests/fault_alloc.c tests/fault_alloc.h include/rbtree.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c tests/fault_alloc.c -o $@
```

Plus `-Itests` added to `CFLAGS` so `#include "fault_alloc.h"` resolves from `src/rbtree.c`
as well as from `tests/*.c` (today only `-Iinclude` is set).

With that, `src/rbtree.c:24-25`'s two `static` definitions are **deleted outright** (not
macro-guarded) and replaced with `#include "fault_alloc.h"`, which declares (not defines)
`rb_malloc`/`rb_free`. Definition site, per target:

| Target | Binary built | Sources linked | Where `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are *defined* |
|---|---|---|---|
| `all` / `test` / `asan` | `build/test_rbtree` | `rbtree.c` (decl only) + `test_rbtree.c` (none) + `fault_alloc.c` (**defines**) | `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exactly once |
| `all` / `test` / `asan` | `build/fuzz` | `rbtree.c` (decl only) + `fuzz.c` (none) + `fault_alloc.c` (**defines**) | `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exactly once |
| `memcheck` | both of the above, under valgrind | same as above | same as above |
| `clean` | builds nothing | — | — |

Every Makefile target that produces a binary links `fault_alloc.c` exactly once alongside
`rbtree.c`'s declaration-only copy — one definition per link, no unresolved symbol, no
duplicate symbol, and no second ("production") build configuration is needed, since there
is no target in this Makefile that builds a binary *without* `tests/fault_alloc.c`. The
"trivially forward to malloc/free in production" language in the spec is satisfied by
`fault_alloc.c`'s own **disarmed** behavior (section 7b), not by a separate source file or
macro — confirming the original `#ifndef RBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC`/separate-sweep-binary design
was unnecessary scaffolding.

### 7b. `tests/fault_alloc.h` / `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exact semantics

Interface (verbatim, per your spec): `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`, `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`,
`fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)`.

Internal state: one call counter (`long calls_since_arm`), one target (`long fail_at`, 0 =
disarmed/never-fail).

- `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`: sets `fail_at = n` (n ≥ 1), resets `calls_since_arm = 0`, and
  enables injection. This is the **only** place the counter resets.
- `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`: sets `fail_at = 0` (no call will ever be injected again).
  It does **not** reset `calls_since_arm` — the spec never promises disarm touches the
  counter, so the design doesn't rely on it doing anything beyond turning injection off.
- `fault_alloc_total(void)`: returns `calls_since_arm` — count of `rb_malloc` calls
  observed since the most recent `fault_alloc_arm()` call, armed or not.
- `rb_malloc(size_t n)`: `calls_since_arm++`; if armed and `calls_since_arm == fail_at`,
  return `NULL` without calling real `malloc`; otherwise forward to real `malloc`.
- `rb_free(void *p)`: always forwards to real `free`, unconditionally — never injected.

**Why "since-last-arm," not lifetime-total or since-last-disarm:** the sweep only ever
needs one fact per iteration — how many `rb_malloc` calls happened during *this* armed
run. `fault_alloc_arm(n)` resetting the counter makes `fault_alloc_total()` at any point
during or after that run answer exactly that, with no dependence on how many allocations
happened in prior iterations or on whether `disarm()` resets anything (which the spec
never specifies). This is sufficient for both checks the sweep needs:
1. When injection fires, `fault_alloc_total() == n` by construction (the counter hits
   `fail_at` at the moment of injection) — nothing more needs to be assumed.
2. When a full scenario replay finishes with no `-1` anywhere, `fault_alloc_total()` at
   that point is the *true total allocations the scenario makes*, which is `< n` by
   definition (if it were `≥ n` injection would already have fired) — this is exactly the
   "run completed without hitting the fault" signal the termination rule needs, with no
   separate lifetime counter required.

### 7c. Deterministic fixed scenario

A small, hand-picked, non-random sequence of `rb_insert` calls, reused identically every
iteration, chosen to trigger at least one rotation/recolor in `insert_fixup` — so the sweep
also demonstrates failures never reach fixup (section 3), not merely that the two
`if`-checks exist. No randomness: every iteration's failing call must be exactly
reproducible and nameable in a failure report.

### 7d. Sweep loop and termination

```
n = 1
loop:
    fault_alloc_arm(n)
    t = rb_create(counting_free)
    if (t == NULL):
        assert fault_alloc_total() == n       # rb_create's own malloc was call n
        n++; continue

    model_before = {}                          # key -> value, built as scenario replays
    hit = false
    for (key, value) in fixed_scenario:
        size_before  = rb_size(t)
        find_before  = rb_find(t, key)          # section 7e, requirement 3
        rc = rb_insert(t, key, value)
        if (rc == -1):
            assert_unchanged(t, model_before, key, find_before, size_before, value)
            assert fault_alloc_total() == n
            hit = true
            break
        model_before[key] = value               # only on success

    rb_destroy(t)
    fault_alloc_disarm()
    if (!hit):
        break                                   # scenario ran to completion untouched -> sweep done
    n++
```

No preliminary dry run to learn a total `N` first — "rerun with the n-th allocation
failing until a run completes without hitting the fault" *is* the termination rule, taken
literally. This also directly answers the `rb_create`-vs-`rb_insert` split (Q6): a failure
landing in `rb_create` has no tree and no model yet, so the only assertions possible/needed
are the `NULL` return and `fault_alloc_total()==n`; a failure landing in `rb_insert` has a
live tree and a partial model built from prior *successful* inserts in this same run, which
is exactly what `assert_unchanged` below checks against.

### 7e. `assert_unchanged` — tightened to the spec's five minimums

Given the model dict (keys successfully inserted so far in *this* run) and the pre-call
snapshot (`size_before`, `find_before` for the about-to-fail key):

1. `rb_validate(t) == 0`.
2. `rb_size(t) == size_before`.

+### 7b. `tests/fault_alloc.h` / `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exact semantics
+Interface (verbatim, per your spec): `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`, `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`,
+`fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)`.
+Internal state: one call counter (`long calls_since_arm`), one target (`long fail_at`, 0 =
+disarmed/never-fail).
+- `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`: sets `fail_at = n` (n ≥ 1), resets `calls_since_arm = 0`, and
+  enables injection. This is the **only** place the counter resets.
+- `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`: sets `fail_at = 0` (no call will ever be injected again).
+  It does **not** reset `calls_since_arm` — the spec never promises disarm touches the
+  counter, so the design doesn't rely on it doing anything beyond turning injection off.
+- `fault_alloc_total(void)`: returns `calls_since_arm` — count of `rb_malloc` calls
+  observed since the most recent `fault_alloc_arm()` call, armed or not.
+- `rb_malloc(size_t n)`: `calls_since_arm++`; if armed and `calls_since_arm == fail_at`,
+  return `NULL` without calling real `malloc`; otherwise forward to real `malloc`.
+- `rb_free(void *p)`: always forwards to real `free`, unconditionally — never injected.
+**Why "since-last-arm," not lifetime-total or since-last-disarm:** the sweep only ever
+needs one fact per iteration — how many `rb_malloc` calls happened during *this* armed
+run. `fault_alloc_arm(n)` resetting the counter makes `fault_alloc_total()` at any point
+during or after that run answer exactly that, with no dependence on how many allocations
+happened in prior iterations or on whether `disarm()` resets anything (which the spec
+never specifies). This is sufficient for both checks the sweep needs:
+1. When injection fires, `fault_alloc_total() == n` by construction (the counter hits
+   `fail_at` at the moment of injection) — nothing more needs to be assumed.
+2. When a full scenario replay finishes with no `-1` anywhere, `fault_alloc_total()` at
+   that point is the *true total allocations the scenario makes*, which is `< n` by
+   definition (if it were `≥ n` injection would already have fired) — this is exactly the
+   "run completed without hitting the fault" signal the termination rule needs, with no
+   separate lifetime counter required.

+A small, hand-picked, non-random sequence of `rb_insert` calls, reused identically every
+iteration, chosen to trigger at least one rotation/recolor in `insert_fixup` — so the sweep
+also demonstrates failures never reach fixup (section 3), not merely that the two
+`if`-checks exist. No randomness: every iteration's failing call must be exactly
+reproducible and nameable in a failure report.
+### 7d. Sweep loop and termination
+loop:
+    fault_alloc_arm(n)
+    t = rb_create(counting_free)
+    if (t == NULL):
+        assert fault_alloc_total() == n       # rb_create's own malloc was call n
+        n++; continue

+    hit = false

1	# Mutation 1 — allocation-failure fault injection: analysis & plan
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	HW2 requires every heap allocation in `src/rbtree.c` to be checked, with every failure
6	leaving the tree byte-for-byte unchanged, caller-owned values still caller-owned, and no
7	leaks (`make asan` / `make memcheck` clean). Today `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are `static`
8	pass-throughs to libc, and `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` are empty stubs. Mutation 1 is the
9	work that turns the seam into something a deterministic fault injector can sit underneath,
10	and proves `rb_insert` (the only non-trivial allocator in the file) is atomic against
11	injected failures. This plan is built from the actual current `src/rbtree.c` /
12	`include/rbtree.h` / `tests/test_rbtree.c` and from CLAUDE.md/NOTES.md — I could not read
13	`CS370-HW2.pdf` directly (no `pdftotext`/`poppler-utils` in this environment), so anything
14	here that assumes Mutation 1's scope boundary should be checked against the PDF's own
15	wording before final sign-off.
16	
17	## 1. Every allocation reachable from `rb_insert`, in source order
18	
19	`rb_insert` (`src/rbtree.c:120-158`):
20	
21	| # | Line | Allocation | Owner immediately after success | On failure | Resource(s) to release |
22	|---|------|------------|----------------------------------|------------|-------------------------|

# Mutation 1 — allocation-failure fault injection: analysis & plan

## Context

HW2 requires every heap allocation in `src/rbtree.c` to be checked, with every failure
leaving the tree byte-for-byte unchanged, caller-owned values still caller-owned, and no
leaks (`make asan` / `make memcheck` clean). Today `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are `static`
pass-throughs to libc, and `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` are empty stubs. Mutation 1 is the
work that turns the seam into something a deterministic fault injector can sit underneath,
and proves `rb_insert` (the only non-trivial allocator in the file) is atomic against
injected failures. This plan is built from the actual current `src/rbtree.c` /
`include/rbtree.h` / `tests/test_rbtree.c` and from CLAUDE.md/NOTES.md — I could not read
`CS370-HW2.pdf` directly (no `pdftotext`/`poppler-utils` in this environment), so anything
here that assumes Mutation 1's scope boundary should be checked against the PDF's own
wording before final sign-off.

## 1. Every allocation reachable from `rb_insert`, in source order

`rb_insert` (`src/rbtree.c:120-158`):

| # | Line | Allocation | Owner immediately after success | On failure | Resource(s) to release |
|---|------|------------|----------------------------------|------------|-------------------------|
| — | 126-129 (overwrite, `cmp==0`) | **none** | n/a | n/a (cannot fail) | n/a |
| 1 | 135 `n = rb_malloc(sizeof *n)` | new node struct | local `n` (not yet linked into the tree) | `return -1` immediately (136) | nothing — this was the only thing acquired, and it never succeeded |
| 2 | 139 `n->key = rb_malloc(keylen)` | key copy | local `n->key` (still not linked into the tree) | `rb_free(n); return -1;` (140-142) | `n` (the node struct from #1) |

No other `rb_malloc` call exists anywhere in `rb_insert`. `rb_create` (line 30-37) has
exactly one more allocation in the whole file (the `rbtree_t` struct itself), fails with
`return NULL` before any state exists, and already needs no unwind.

## 2. Candidate commit point

Line 151-153:
```c
if (parent == NULL)      t->root = n;
else if (cmp < 0)        parent->left = n;
else                     parent->right = n;
```
This is the **first** line that mutates the tree itself (first write to `t->root` or to an
existing node's `left`/`right`). Everything before it — both `rb_malloc` calls, `memcpy`,
and populating `n`'s fields — touches only the new, not-yet-linked node.

## 3. Failure points vs. the commit point

Both allocation failure points (#1 and #2 above) occur **strictly before** line 151 — by
construction, since both `rb_malloc` calls happen textually earlier and nothing branches
back. Consequence: **`insert_fixup` can never run on a failed `rb_insert`** — it is only
called (line 155) after the unconditional link-in, so there is no fixup-reachable fault
path to worry about at all for Mutation 1. There are no failure points after the commit
point in the current code, and none should be introduced.

## 4. Error-path structure

**No new structure is needed.** The acquire-everything-before-mutating-anything ordering
already gives failure atomicity for free: at every failure point there is at most one
resource to release (none for #1, just `n` for #2), and the existing plain
`if (... == NULL) { cleanup; return -1; }` pairs already do that, LIFO, with no reordering
required. Per CLAUDE.md ("do not add cleanup paths that can instead be designed away") and
the house goto-cleanup rule (reserved for *multi-step* unwinds), introducing a
`goto cleanup` label here would be unneeded ceremony for a single-step release — recommend
leaving this exactly as-is. Flagging this as a judgment call since you said you'd push
back: if the grading rubric wants goto-cleanup unconditionally for any function with ≥2
allocations regardless of unwind complexity, that's a style call to settle explicitly.

## 5. Overwrite-existing-key path (lines 126-129)

- **Allocates today?** No — `cmp == 0` returns before either `rb_malloc` call.
- **Needs to allocate?** No — the key already matches via `strcmp`, so no new key copy or
  node is ever needed.
- **Old value ownership:** the tree already owns it (absorbed on a prior successful
  insert); `t->value_free(cur->value)` (line 127) is the tree releasing its own property,
  matching the header's "sole owner at that instant" contract.
- **New value ownership transfer:** immediate and unconditional at line 128
  (`cur->value = value`) — since this path cannot fail, there is no partial-ownership
  window to protect. This means the overwrite path has **zero allocation-failure modes**
  under Mutation 1; the fault injector should have nothing to inject here, and a test
  should affirmatively prove that (section 8, item 4).

## 6. `rb_delete` allocation surface

Full read of `rb_delete`/`transplant`/`delete_fixup` (lines 188-284): no call to
`rb_malloc` anywhere — only `rb_free` (lines 255, 278, 281). `rb_delete` must gain no new
allocation-failure mode in Mutation 1, and today it has none to begin with. A fault
injector set to fail on the very next allocation should still let `rb_delete` succeed,
since it never asks the allocator for anything (test in section 8, item 6).

## 7. Fault-sweep harness design

### 7a. Seam linkage — exact definition site per Makefile target

Current `Makefile` link lines (confirmed by re-reading it, not the HW2 starter — see the
note at the top of this plan: no separate starter Makefile file exists in this repo and I
have no PDF-text access to CS370-HW2.pdf in this environment, so this trace is against the
actual current `Makefile` only):

```
$(BIN):     $(CC) $(TEST_CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC)         -o $@   # src/rbtree.c + tests/test_rbtree.c
$(FUZZBIN): $(CC) $(CFLAGS)      $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c    -o $@   # src/rbtree.c + tests/fuzz.c
```

Neither currently lists `tests/fault_alloc.c`. Required edit: add `tests/fault_alloc.c` to
*both* link lines (and as a prerequisite, alongside `tests/fault_alloc.h`, so touching the
injector triggers a rebuild):

```
$(BIN):     $(SRC) $(TSRC) tests/fault_alloc.c tests/fault_alloc.h include/rbtree.h
	$(CC) $(TEST_CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC) tests/fault_alloc.c -o $@

$(FUZZBIN): $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c tests/fault_alloc.c tests/fault_alloc.h include/rbtree.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c tests/fault_alloc.c -o $@
```

Plus `-Itests` added to `CFLAGS` so `#include "fault_alloc.h"` resolves from `src/rbtree.c`
as well as from `tests/*.c` (today only `-Iinclude` is set).

With that, `src/rbtree.c:24-25`'s two `static` definitions are **deleted outright** (not
macro-guarded) and replaced with `#include "fault_alloc.h"`, which declares (not defines)
`rb_malloc`/`rb_free`. Definition site, per target:

| Target | Binary built | Sources linked | Where `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are *defined* |
|---|---|---|---|
| `all` / `test` / `asan` | `build/test_rbtree` | `rbtree.c` (decl only) + `test_rbtree.c` (none) + `fault_alloc.c` (**defines**) | `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exactly once |
| `all` / `test` / `asan` | `build/fuzz` | `rbtree.c` (decl only) + `fuzz.c` (none) + `fault_alloc.c` (**defines**) | `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exactly once |
| `memcheck` | both of the above, under valgrind | same as above | same as above |
| `clean` | builds nothing | — | — |

Every Makefile target that produces a binary links `fault_alloc.c` exactly once alongside
`rbtree.c`'s declaration-only copy — one definition per link, no unresolved symbol, no
duplicate symbol, and no second ("production") build configuration is needed, since there
is no target in this Makefile that builds a binary *without* `tests/fault_alloc.c`. The
"trivially forward to malloc/free in production" language in the spec is satisfied by
`fault_alloc.c`'s own **disarmed** behavior (section 7b), not by a separate source file or
macro — confirming the original `#ifndef RBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC`/separate-sweep-binary design
was unnecessary scaffolding.

### 7b. `tests/fault_alloc.h` / `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exact semantics

Interface (verbatim, per your spec): `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`, `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`,
`fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)`.

Internal state: one call counter (`long calls_since_arm`), one target (`long fail_at`, 0 =
disarmed/never-fail).

- `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`: sets `fail_at = n` (n ≥ 1), resets `calls_since_arm = 0`, and
  enables injection. This is the **only** place the counter resets.
- `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`: sets `fail_at = 0` (no call will ever be injected again).
  It does **not** reset `calls_since_arm` — the spec never promises disarm touches the
  counter, so the design doesn't rely on it doing anything beyond turning injection off.
- `fault_alloc_total(void)`: returns `calls_since_arm` — count of `rb_malloc` calls
  observed since the most recent `fault_alloc_arm()` call, armed or not.
- `rb_malloc(size_t n)`: `calls_since_arm++`; if armed and `calls_since_arm == fail_at`,
  return `NULL` without calling real `malloc`; otherwise forward to real `malloc`.
- `rb_free(void *p)`: always forwards to real `free`, unconditionally — never injected.

**Why "since-last-arm," not lifetime-total or since-last-disarm:** the sweep only ever
needs one fact per iteration — how many `rb_malloc` calls happened during *this* armed
run. `fault_alloc_arm(n)` resetting the counter makes `fault_alloc_total()` at any point
during or after that run answer exactly that, with no dependence on how many allocations
happened in prior iterations or on whether `disarm()` resets anything (which the spec
never specifies). This is sufficient for both checks the sweep needs:
1. When injection fires, `fault_alloc_total() == n` by construction (the counter hits
   `fail_at` at the moment of injection) — nothing more needs to be assumed.
2. When a full scenario replay finishes with no `-1` anywhere, `fault_alloc_total()` at
   that point is the *true total allocations the scenario makes*, which is `< n` by
   definition (if it were `≥ n` injection would already have fired) — this is exactly the
   "run completed without hitting the fault" signal the termination rule needs, with no
   separate lifetime counter required.

### 7c. Deterministic fixed scenario

A small, hand-picked, non-random sequence of `rb_insert` calls, reused identically every
iteration, chosen to trigger at least one rotation/recolor in `insert_fixup` — so the sweep
also demonstrates failures never reach fixup (section 3), not merely that the two
`if`-checks exist. No randomness: every iteration's failing call must be exactly
reproducible and nameable in a failure report.

### 7d. Sweep loop and termination

```
n = 1
loop:
    fault_alloc_arm(n)
    t = rb_create(counting_free)
    if (t == NULL):
        assert fault_alloc_total() == n       # rb_create's own malloc was call n
        n++; continue

    model_before = {}                          # key -> value, built as scenario replays
    hit = false
    for (key, value) in fixed_scenario:
        size_before  = rb_size(t)
        find_before  = rb_find(t, key)          # section 7e, requirement 3
        rc = rb_insert(t, key, value)
        if (rc == -1):
            assert_unchanged(t, model_before, key, find_before, size_before, value)
            assert fault_alloc_total() == n
            hit = true
            break
        model_before[key] = value               # only on success

    rb_destroy(t)
    fault_alloc_disarm()
    if (!hit):
        break                                   # scenario ran to completion untouched -> sweep done
    n++
```

No preliminary dry run to learn a total `N` first — "rerun with the n-th allocation
failing until a run completes without hitting the fault" *is* the termination rule, taken
literally. This also directly answers the `rb_create`-vs-`rb_insert` split (Q6): a failure
landing in `rb_create` has no tree and no model yet, so the only assertions possible/needed
are the `NULL` return and `fault_alloc_total()==n`; a failure landing in `rb_insert` has a
live tree and a partial model built from prior *successful* inserts in this same run, which
is exactly what `assert_unchanged` below checks against.

### 7e. `assert_unchanged` — tightened to the spec's five minimums

Given the model dict (keys successfully inserted so far in *this* run) and the pre-call
snapshot (`size_before`, `find_before` for the about-to-fail key):

1. `rb_validate(t) == 0`.
2. `rb_size(t) == size_before`.
3. `rb_find(t, failed_key) == find_before` (for a brand-new key this is `NULL` both times;

4. For every other key already in `model_before`: `rb_find(t, other_key) == model_before[other_key]`.
5. The counting destructor's call count (`free_count`, reusing the existing
   `tests/test_rbtree.c:69-94` pattern) is unchanged from immediately before the call —
   the caller-owned `value` passed to the failed `rb_insert` was never freed by the tree.

### 7f. Value ownership *inside the harness itself*

The harness must not leak the thing it's using to prove the tree doesn't leak. When
`rb_insert(t, key, value_ptr)` returns `-1`, the tree never absorbed `value_ptr` — ownership
stayed with the caller, i.e. with the harness. If `value_ptr` was heap-allocated (it must
be, so a counting/tagged destructor can tell absorbed from not), **the harness is now the
only thing that will ever free it**, since `rb_destroy(t)` only calls `value_free` on nodes
the tree actually holds.

Concretely, per sweep iteration (section 7d): the scenario's values are generated fresh
each iteration (a small factory called right before each `rb_insert`, not a shared array
reused across iterations — once one iteration's tree absorbs and later destroys a value,
that value is gone; it can't be reused by the next `n`). Exactly one value per iteration is
ever at risk: the one passed to the call that fails (the loop breaks on the first `-1`, so
at most one failed insert per iteration). Immediately after `assert_unchanged` confirms the
tree didn't touch it:

```
if (rc == -1) {
    assert_unchanged(...);        // includes: destructor call count unchanged
    assert(fault_alloc_total() == n);
    free(value_ptr);              // harness, as caller, reclaims what it still owns
    hit = true;
    break;
}
model_before[key] = value_ptr;    // tree now owns it; rb_destroy(t)'s value_free will free it
```

Note `free(value_ptr)` here is a **plain `free`**, not the counting destructor passed to
`rb_create` — the tree never owned this value, so routing it through `value_free` would
misreport the destructor-call-count used elsewhere to prove non-absorption, and would risk
being confused with a tree-driven free. Every other value in `model_before` is tree-owned
and is reclaimed exactly once, by `rb_destroy(t)`'s call to `value_free` at the end of the
iteration. This is what makes the sweep run clean under `make asan`/`make memcheck`: every
value is freed exactly once, either by the harness (rejected values) or by the tree
(absorbed values), never both, never neither.
