# Mutation 1 — allocation-failure fault injection: analysis & plan

## Context

HW2 requires every heap allocation in `src/rbtree.c` to be checked, with every failure
leaving the tree byte-for-byte unchanged, caller-owned values still caller-owned, and no
leaks (`make asan` / `make memcheck` clean). Today `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are `static`
pass-throughs to libc, and `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` are empty stubs. Mutation 1 is the
work that turns the seam into something a deterministic fault injector can sit underneath,
and proves `rb_insert` (the only non-trivial allocator in the file) is atomic against
injected failures. This plan is built from the actual current `src/rbtree.c` /
`include/rbtree.h` / `tests/test_rbtree.c` and from CLAUDE.md/NOTES.md — I could not read
`CS370-HW2.pdf` directly (no `pdftotext`/`poppler-utils` in this environment), so anything
here that assumes Mutation 1's scope boundary should be checked against the PDF's own
wording before final sign-off.

## 1. Every allocation reachable from `rb_insert`, in source order

`rb_insert` (`src/rbtree.c:120-158`):

| # | Line | Allocation | Owner immediately after success | On failure | Resource(s) to release |
|---|------|------------|----------------------------------|------------|-------------------------|
| — | 126-129 (overwrite, `cmp==0`) | **none** | n/a | n/a (cannot fail) | n/a |
| 1 | 135 `n = rb_malloc(sizeof *n)` | new node struct | local `n` (not yet linked into the tree) | `return -1` immediately (136) | nothing — this was the only thing acquired, and it never succeeded |
| 2 | 139 `n->key = rb_malloc(keylen)` | key copy | local `n->key` (still not linked into the tree) | `rb_free(n); return -1;` (140-142) | `n` (the node struct from #1) |

No other `rb_malloc` call exists anywhere in `rb_insert`. `rb_create` (line 30-37) has
exactly one more allocation in the whole file (the `rbtree_t` struct itself), fails with
`return NULL` before any state exists, and already needs no unwind.

## 2. Candidate commit point

Line 151-153:
```c
if (parent == NULL)      t->root = n;
else if (cmp < 0)        parent->left = n;
else                     parent->right = n;
```
This is the **first** line that mutates the tree itself (first write to `t->root` or to an
existing node's `left`/`right`). Everything before it — both `rb_malloc` calls, `memcpy`,
and populating `n`'s fields — touches only the new, not-yet-linked node.

## 3. Failure points vs. the commit point

Both allocation failure points (#1 and #2 above) occur **strictly before** line 151 — by
construction, since both `rb_malloc` calls happen textually earlier and nothing branches
back. Consequence: **`insert_fixup` can never run on a failed `rb_insert`** — it is only
called (line 155) after the unconditional link-in, so there is no fixup-reachable fault
path to worry about at all for Mutation 1. There are no failure points after the commit
point in the current code, and none should be introduced.

## 4. Error-path structure

**No new structure is needed.** The acquire-everything-before-mutating-anything ordering
already gives failure atomicity for free: at every failure point there is at most one
resource to release (none for #1, just `n` for #2), and the existing plain
`if (... == NULL) { cleanup; return -1; }` pairs already do that, LIFO, with no reordering
required. Per CLAUDE.md ("do not add cleanup paths that can instead be designed away") and
the house goto-cleanup rule (reserved for *multi-step* unwinds), introducing a
`goto cleanup` label here would be unneeded ceremony for a single-step release — recommend
leaving this exactly as-is. Flagging this as a judgment call since you said you'd push
back: if the grading rubric wants goto-cleanup unconditionally for any function with ≥2
allocations regardless of unwind complexity, that's a style call to settle explicitly.

## 5. Overwrite-existing-key path (lines 126-129)

- **Allocates today?** No — `cmp == 0` returns before either `rb_malloc` call.
- **Needs to allocate?** No — the key already matches via `strcmp`, so no new key copy or
  node is ever needed.
- **Old value ownership:** the tree already owns it (absorbed on a prior successful
  insert); `t->value_free(cur->value)` (line 127) is the tree releasing its own property,
  matching the header's "sole owner at that instant" contract.
- **New value ownership transfer:** immediate and unconditional at line 128
  (`cur->value = value`) — since this path cannot fail, there is no partial-ownership
  window to protect. This means the overwrite path has **zero allocation-failure modes**
  under Mutation 1; the fault injector should have nothing to inject here, and a test
  should affirmatively prove that (section 8, item 4).

## 6. `rb_delete` allocation surface

Full read of `rb_delete`/`transplant`/`delete_fixup` (lines 188-284): no call to
`rb_malloc` anywhere — only `rb_free` (lines 255, 278, 281). `rb_delete` must gain no new
allocation-failure mode in Mutation 1, and today it has none to begin with. A fault
injector set to fail on the very next allocation should still let `rb_delete` succeed,
since it never asks the allocator for anything (test in section 8, item 6).

## 7. Fault-sweep harness design

### 7a. Seam linkage — exact definition site per Makefile target

Current `Makefile` link lines (confirmed by re-reading it, not the HW2 starter — see the
note at the top of this plan: no separate starter Makefile file exists in this repo and I
have no PDF-text access to CS370-HW2.pdf in this environment, so this trace is against the
actual current `Makefile` only):

```
$(BIN):     $(CC) $(TEST_CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC)         -o $@   # src/rbtree.c + tests/test_rbtree.c
$(FUZZBIN): $(CC) $(CFLAGS)      $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c    -o $@   # src/rbtree.c + tests/fuzz.c
```

Neither currently lists `tests/fault_alloc.c`. Required edit: add `tests/fault_alloc.c` to
*both* link lines (and as a prerequisite, alongside `tests/fault_alloc.h`, so touching the
injector triggers a rebuild):

```
$(BIN):     $(SRC) $(TSRC) tests/fault_alloc.c tests/fault_alloc.h include/rbtree.h
	$(CC) $(TEST_CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC) tests/fault_alloc.c -o $@

$(FUZZBIN): $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c tests/fault_alloc.c tests/fault_alloc.h include/rbtree.h
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c tests/fault_alloc.c -o $@
```

Plus `-Itests` added to `CFLAGS` so `#include "fault_alloc.h"` resolves from `src/rbtree.c`
as well as from `tests/*.c` (today only `-Iinclude` is set).

With that, `src/rbtree.c:24-25`'s two `static` definitions are **deleted outright** (not
macro-guarded) and replaced with `#include "fault_alloc.h"`, which declares (not defines)

### 7b. `tests/fault_alloc.h` / `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exact semantics

Interface (verbatim, per your spec): `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`, `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`,
`fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)`.

Internal state: one call counter (`long calls_since_arm`), one target (`long fail_at`, 0 =
disarmed/never-fail).

- `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`: sets `fail_at = n` (n ≥ 1), resets `calls_since_arm = 0`, and
  enables injection. This is the **only** place the counter resets.
- `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`: sets `fail_at = 0` (no call will ever be injected again).
  It does **not** reset `calls_since_arm` — the spec never promises disarm touches the
  counter, so the design doesn't rely on it doing anything beyond turning injection off.
- `fault_alloc_total(void)`: returns `calls_since_arm` — count of `rb_malloc` calls
  observed since the most recent `fault_alloc_arm()` call, armed or not.
- `rb_malloc(size_t n)`: `calls_since_arm++`; if armed and `calls_since_arm == fail_at`,
  return `NULL` without calling real `malloc`; otherwise forward to real `malloc`.
- `rb_free(void *p)`: always forwards to real `free`, unconditionally — never injected.

**Why "since-last-arm," not lifetime-total or since-last-disarm:** the sweep only ever
needs one fact per iteration — how many `rb_malloc` calls happened during *this* armed
run. `fault_alloc_arm(n)` resetting the counter makes `fault_alloc_total()` at any point
during or after that run answer exactly that, with no dependence on how many allocations
happened in prior iterations or on whether `disarm()` resets anything (which the spec
never specifies). This is sufficient for both checks the sweep needs:
1. When injection fires, `fault_alloc_total() == n` by construction (the counter hits
   `fail_at` at the moment of injection) — nothing more needs to be assumed.
2. When a full scenario replay finishes with no `-1` anywhere, `fault_alloc_total()` at
   that point is the *true total allocations the scenario makes*, which is `< n` by
   definition (if it were `≥ n` injection would already have fired) — this is exactly the
   "run completed without hitting the fault" signal the termination rule needs, with no
   separate lifetime counter required.

### 7c. Deterministic fixed scenario

A small, hand-picked, non-random sequence of `rb_insert` calls, reused identically every
iteration, chosen to trigger at least one rotation/recolor in `insert_fixup` — so the sweep
also demonstrates failures never reach fixup (section 3), not merely that the two
`if`-checks exist. No randomness: every iteration's failing call must be exactly
reproducible and nameable in a failure report.

### 7d. Sweep loop and termination

```
n = 1
loop:
    fault_alloc_arm(n)
    t = rb_create(counting_free)
    if (t == NULL):
        assert fault_alloc_total() == n       # rb_create's own malloc was call n
        n++; continue

    model_before = {}                          # key -> value, built as scenario replays
    hit = false
    for (key, value) in fixed_scenario:
        size_before  = rb_size(t)
        find_before  = rb_find(t, key)          # section 7e, requirement 3
        rc = rb_insert(t, key, value)
        if (rc == -1):
            assert_unchanged(t, model_before, key, find_before, size_before, value)
            assert fault_alloc_total() == n
            hit = true
            break
        model_before[key] = value               # only on success

    rb_destroy(t)
    fault_alloc_disarm()
    if (!hit):
        break                                   # scenario ran to completion untouched -> sweep done
    n++
```

No preliminary dry run to learn a total `N` first — "rerun with the n-th allocation
failing until a run completes without hitting the fault" *is* the termination rule, taken
literally. This also directly answers the `rb_create`-vs-`rb_insert` split (Q6): a failure
landing in `rb_create` has no tree and no model yet, so the only assertions possible/needed
are the `NULL` return and `fault_alloc_total()==n`; a failure landing in `rb_insert` has a
live tree and a partial model built from prior *successful* inserts in this same run, which
is exactly what `assert_unchanged` below checks against.

### 7e. `assert_unchanged` — tightened to the spec's five minimums

Given the model dict (keys successfully inserted so far in *this* run) and the pre-call
snapshot (`size_before`, `find_before` for the about-to-fail key):

1. `rb_validate(t) == 0`.
2. `rb_size(t) == size_before`.
3. `rb_find(t, failed_key) == find_before` (for a brand-new key this is `NULL` both times;
   for a failing overwrite it's the prior value, unchanged).
4. For every other key already in `model_before`: `rb_find(t, other_key) == model_before[other_key]`.
5. The counting destructor's call count (`free_count`, reusing the existing
   `tests/test_rbtree.c:69-94` pattern) is unchanged from immediately before the call —
   the caller-owned `value` passed to the failed `rb_insert` was never freed by the tree.

`rb_size`/`rb_validate`/the destructor counter is the spec's exact minimum and is simpler
than the in-order-dump approach from the previous revision.

### 7f. Value ownership *inside the harness itself*

The harness must not leak the thing it's using to prove the tree doesn't leak. When
`rb_insert(t, key, value_ptr)` returns `-1`, the tree never absorbed `value_ptr` — ownership
stayed with the caller, i.e. with the harness. If `value_ptr` was heap-allocated (it must
be, so a counting/tagged destructor can tell absorbed from not), **the harness is now the
only thing that will ever free it**, since `rb_destroy(t)` only calls `value_free` on nodes
the tree actually holds.

Concretely, per sweep iteration (section 7d): the scenario's values are generated fresh
each iteration (a small factory called right before each `rb_insert`, not a shared array
reused across iterations — once one iteration's tree absorbs and later destroys a value,
that value is gone; it can't be reused by the next `n`). Exactly one value per iteration is
ever at risk: the one passed to the call that fails (the loop breaks on the first `-1`, so
at most one failed insert per iteration). Immediately after `assert_unchanged` confirms the
tree didn't touch it:

```
if (rc == -1) {
    assert_unchanged(...);        // includes: destructor call count unchanged
    assert(fault_alloc_total() == n);
    free(value_ptr);              // harness, as caller, reclaims what it still owns
    hit = true;
    break;
}
model_before[key] = value_ptr;    // tree now owns it; rb_destroy(t)'s value_free will free it
```

`rb_create` — the tree never owned this value, so routing it through `value_free` would
misreport the destructor-call-count used elsewhere to prove non-absorption, and would risk
being confused with a tree-driven free. Every other value in `model_before` is tree-owned
and is reclaimed exactly once, by `rb_destroy(t)`'s call to `value_free` at the end of the
iteration. This is what makes the sweep run clean under `make asan`/`make memcheck`: every
value is freed exactly once, either by the harness (rejected values) or by the tree
(absorbed values), never both, never neither.

name: rbtree-lab-plan-rigor
description: User cross-checks every plan claim against the actual current repo files (not the PDF spec's prose or assumed starter state) and rejects plans with logical sequencing errors, even subtle ones.
metadata:

---

Before a plan is approved in this project, expect it to be checked line-by-line against
the real current state of `Makefile`, `src/rbtree.c`, `include/rbtree.h`, and
`tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` — not against what the HW2 PDF says should exist, and not against
assumptions carried over from a previous plan draft. Re-read the actual files fresh each
time a plan claims something about "current" wiring (e.g. don't assume a Makefile already
links a file just because the assignment implies it should).

**Why:** During the Mutation 1 fault-injection plan, the user caught: (1) a claim that the
Makefile "already links tests/fault_alloc.c" that didn't match the actual (empty,
unlinked) files; (2) a sweep-termination design (`if (!hit) break`) that silently conflated
"the API returned -1" with "the injected allocation was actually reached," which would let
a buggy API that swallows a NULL allocation and returns success falsely look like a
legitimate sweep-completion case; (3) a tests-before-code task list where the tests
couldn't actually pass yet because the seam-wiring edit they depended on was listed last.
None of these were caught by surface review — they required tracing the actual mechanics.

**How to apply:** Re-read the real file contents before asserting what they currently do,
distinguish "returned an error code" from "the specific fault being tested for actually
fired" when designing fault-injection/property tests, and double check that a tests-first
ordering is genuinely executable in the order written (a test placed before a prerequisite
production change is not actually tests-first, even if it's labeled that way). See
[[feedback-slices-tests-leading]] for the related ordering/slicing expectation.

# Mutation 1 — allocation-failure fault injection: analysis & plan

## Context

HW2 requires every heap allocation in `src/rbtree.c` to be checked, with every failure
leaving the tree byte-for-byte unchanged, caller-owned values still caller-owned, and no
leaks (`make asan` / `make memcheck` clean). Today `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are `static`
pass-throughs to libc, and `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` are empty stubs. Mutation 1 is the
work that turns the seam into something a deterministic fault injector can sit underneath,
and proves `rb_insert` (the only non-trivial allocator in the file) is atomic against
injected failures. This plan is built from the actual current `src/rbtree.c` /
`include/rbtree.h` / `tests/test_rbtree.c` and from CLAUDE.md/NOTES.md — I could not read
`CS370-HW2.pdf` directly (no `pdftotext`/`poppler-utils` in this environment), so anything
here that assumes Mutation 1's scope boundary should be checked against the PDF's own
wording before final sign-off.

## 1. Every allocation reachable from `rb_insert`, in source order

`rb_insert` (`src/rbtree.c:120-158`):

| # | Line | Allocation | Owner immediately after success | On failure | Resource(s) to release |
|---|------|------------|----------------------------------|------------|-------------------------|
| — | 126-129 (overwrite, `cmp==0`) | **none** | n/a | n/a (cannot fail) | n/a |
| 1 | 135 `n = rb_malloc(sizeof *n)` | new node struct | local `n` (not yet linked into the tree) | `return -1` immediately (136) | nothing — this was the only thing acquired, and it never succeeded |
| 2 | 139 `n->key = rb_malloc(keylen)` | key copy | local `n->key` (still not linked into the tree) | `rb_free(n); return -1;` (140-142) | `n` (the node struct from #1) |

No other `rb_malloc` call exists anywhere in `rb_insert`. `rb_create` (line 30-37) has
exactly one more allocation in the whole file (the `rbtree_t` struct itself), fails with
`return NULL` before any state exists, and already needs no unwind.

## 2. Candidate commit point

Line 151-153:
```c
if (parent == NULL)      t->root = n;
else if (cmp < 0)        parent->left = n;
else                     parent->right = n;
```
This is the **first** line that mutates the tree itself (first write to `t->root` or to an
existing node's `left`/`right`). Everything before it — both `rb_malloc` calls, `memcpy`,
and populating `n`'s fields — touches only the new, not-yet-linked node.

## 3. Failure points vs. the commit point

Both allocation failure points (#1 and #2 above) occur **strictly before** line 151 — by
construction, since both `rb_malloc` calls happen textually earlier and nothing branches
back. Consequence: **`insert_fixup` can never run on a failed `rb_insert`** — it is only
called (line 155) after the unconditional link-in, so there is no fixup-reachable fault
path to worry about at all for Mutation 1. There are no failure points after the commit
point in the current code, and none should be introduced.

## 4. Error-path structure

**No new structure is needed.** The acquire-everything-before-mutating-anything ordering
already gives failure atomicity for free: at every failure point there is at most one
resource to release (none for #1, just `n` for #2), and the existing plain
`if (... == NULL) { cleanup; return -1; }` pairs already do that, LIFO, with no reordering
required. Per CLAUDE.md ("do not add cleanup paths that can instead be designed away") and
the house goto-cleanup rule (reserved for *multi-step* unwinds), introducing a
`goto cleanup` label here would be unneeded ceremony for a single-step release — recommend
leaving this exactly as-is. Flagging this as a judgment call since you said you'd push
back: if the grading rubric wants goto-cleanup unconditionally for any function with ≥2
allocations regardless of unwind complexity, that's a style call to settle explicitly.

## 5. Overwrite-existing-key path (lines 126-129)

- **Allocates today?** No — `cmp == 0` returns before either `rb_malloc` call.
- **Needs to allocate?** No — the key already matches via `strcmp`, so no new key copy or
  node is ever needed.
- **Old value ownership:** the tree already owns it (absorbed on a prior successful
  insert); `t->value_free(cur->value)` (line 127) is the tree releasing its own property,
  matching the header's "sole owner at that instant" contract.
- **New value ownership transfer:** immediate and unconditional at line 128
  (`cur->value = value`) — since this path cannot fail, there is no partial-ownership
  window to protect. This means the overwrite path has **zero allocation-failure modes**
  under Mutation 1; the fault injector should have nothing to inject here, and a test
  should affirmatively prove that (section 8, item 4).

## 6. `rb_delete` allocation surface

Full read of `rb_delete`/`transplant`/`delete_fixup` (lines 188-284): no call to
`rb_malloc` anywhere — only `rb_free` (lines 255, 278, 281). `rb_delete` must gain no new
allocation-failure mode in Mutation 1, and today it has none to begin with. A fault
injector set to fail on the very next allocation should still let `rb_delete` succeed,
since it never asks the allocator for anything (test in section 8, item 6).

## 7. Fault-sweep harness design

### 7a. Seam linkage — exact definition site per Makefile target

Current `Makefile` link lines (confirmed by re-reading it, not the HW2 starter — see the
note at the top of this plan: no separate starter Makefile file exists in this repo and I

### 7b. `tests/fault_alloc.h` / `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exact semantics

Interface (verbatim, per your spec): `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`, `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`,
`fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)`.

Internal state: one call counter (`long calls_since_arm`), one target (`long fail_at`, 0 =
disarmed/never-fail).

- `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`: sets `fail_at = n` (n ≥ 1), resets `calls_since_arm = 0`, and
  enables injection. This is the **only** place the counter resets.
- `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`: sets `fail_at = 0` (no call will ever be injected again).
  It does **not** reset `calls_since_arm` — the spec never promises disarm touches the
  counter, so the design doesn't rely on it doing anything beyond turning injection off.
- `fault_alloc_total(void)`: returns `calls_since_arm` — count of `rb_malloc` calls
  observed since the most recent `fault_alloc_arm()` call, armed or not.
- `rb_malloc(size_t n)`: `calls_since_arm++`; if armed and `calls_since_arm == fail_at`,
  return `NULL` without calling real `malloc`; otherwise forward to real `malloc`.
- `rb_free(void *p)`: always forwards to real `free`, unconditionally — never injected.

**Why "since-last-arm," not lifetime-total or since-last-disarm:** the sweep only ever
needs one fact per iteration — how many `rb_malloc` calls happened during *this* armed
run. `fault_alloc_arm(n)` resetting the counter makes `fault_alloc_total()` at any point
during or after that run answer exactly that, with no dependence on how many allocations
happened in prior iterations or on whether `disarm()` resets anything (which the spec
never specifies). This is sufficient for both checks the sweep needs:
1. When injection fires, `fault_alloc_total() == n` by construction (the counter hits
   `fail_at` at the moment of injection) — nothing more needs to be assumed.
2. When a full scenario replay finishes with no `-1` anywhere, `fault_alloc_total()` at
   that point is the *true total allocations the scenario makes*, which is `< n` by
   definition (if it were `≥ n` injection would already have fired) — this is exactly the
   "run completed without hitting the fault" signal the termination rule needs, with no
   separate lifetime counter required.

### 7c. Deterministic fixed scenario

A small, hand-picked, non-random sequence of `rb_insert` calls, reused identically every
iteration, chosen to trigger at least one rotation/recolor in `insert_fixup` — so the sweep
also demonstrates failures never reach fixup (section 3), not merely that the two
`if`-checks exist. No randomness: every iteration's failing call must be exactly
reproducible and nameable in a failure report.

### 7d. Sweep loop and termination

```
n = 1
loop:
    fault_alloc_arm(n)
    t = rb_create(counting_free)
    if (t == NULL):
        assert fault_alloc_total() == n       # rb_create's own malloc was call n
        n++; continue

    model_before = {}                          # key -> value, built as scenario replays
    observed_failure = false
    for (key, value) in fixed_scenario:
        size_before  = rb_size(t)
        find_before  = rb_find(t, key)          # section 7e, requirement 3
        rc = rb_insert(t, key, value)
        if (rc == -1):
            assert fault_alloc_total() == n
            assert_unchanged(t, model_before, key, find_before, size_before, value)
            observed_failure = true
            break
        model_before[key] = value               # only on success

    total = fault_alloc_total()                 # read before disarm (disarm doesn't touch it anyway)
    rb_destroy(t)
    fault_alloc_disarm()

    if (total < n):
        # allocation n was never reached by anything in the scenario -- the legitimate
        # termination condition, per the spec's "until a run completes without hitting
        # the fault." This must coincide with observed_failure == false; if the scenario
        # ran dry (total < n) yet we somehow saw an rc == -1 earlier, that is itself a bug
        # to report (a -1 return not explained by any injected allocation failure).
        assert !observed_failure
        break                                   # sweep done
    else:
        # total >= n: the injected allocation WAS reached. The corresponding call is
        # REQUIRED to have returned its documented error code -- if observed_failure is
        # still false here, some API call swallowed a NULL from rb_malloc and returned
        # success anyway. That is a correctness bug the harness must fail the test on,
        # not a reason to treat the sweep as finished.
        assert observed_failure
        n++
```

Note the earlier draft's `if (!hit) break` conflated two different things: "rc == -1 never
happened" was being read as "allocation n was never reached," but those only coincide when
the API under test is correct. Using `fault_alloc_total()` against `n` (not merely whether
`-1` was ever returned) is what actually distinguishes "legitimately finished" from "a
buggy call silently absorbed a failed allocation" — the latter must fail the test, not end
the sweep. This also still answers the `rb_create`-vs-`rb_insert` split (Q6) the same way:
a failure landing in `rb_create` has no tree/model yet, so only the `NULL` return and
`fault_alloc_total()==n` are checked; one landing in `rb_insert` has a live tree and a
partial model from prior successful inserts in this run, checked by `assert_unchanged`.

### 7e. `assert_unchanged` — tightened to the spec's five minimums

Given the model dict (keys successfully inserted so far in *this* run) and the pre-call
snapshot (`size_before`, `find_before` for the about-to-fail key):

1. `rb_validate(t) == 0`.
2. `rb_size(t) == size_before`.
3. `rb_find(t, failed_key) == find_before` (for a brand-new key this is `NULL` both times;
   for a failing overwrite it's the prior value, unchanged).
4. For every other key already in `model_before`: `rb_find(t, other_key) == model_before[other_key]`.
5. The counting destructor's call count (`free_count`, reusing the existing
   `tests/test_rbtree.c:69-94` pattern) is unchanged from immediately before the call —
   the caller-owned `value` passed to the failed `rb_insert` was never freed by the tree.

No full in-order snapshot/array capture is needed — `rb_find` against the model plus
`rb_size`/`rb_validate`/the destructor counter is the spec's exact minimum and is simpler
than the in-order-dump approach from the previous revision.

### 7f. Value ownership *inside the harness itself*

The harness must not leak the thing it's using to prove the tree doesn't leak. When
`rb_insert(t, key, value_ptr)` returns `-1`, the tree never absorbed `value_ptr` — ownership
stayed with the caller, i.e. with the harness. If `value_ptr` was heap-allocated (it must
be, so a counting/tagged destructor can tell absorbed from not), **the harness is now the
only thing that will ever free it**, since `rb_destroy(t)` only calls `value_free` on nodes
the tree actually holds.

Concretely, per sweep iteration (section 7d): the scenario's values are generated fresh
each iteration (a small factory called right before each `rb_insert`, not a shared array
reused across iterations — once one iteration's tree absorbs and later destroys a value,
that value is gone; it can't be reused by the next `n`). Exactly one value per iteration is
ever at risk: the one passed to the call that fails (the loop breaks on the first `-1`, so
at most one failed insert per iteration). Immediately after `assert_unchanged` confirms the
tree didn't touch it:

```
rc = rb_insert(t, key, value_ptr);
if (rc == -1) {
    assert_unchanged(...);        // includes: destructor call count unchanged
    assert(fault_alloc_total() == n);
    free(value_ptr);              // harness, as caller, reclaims what it still owns
    hit = true;
    break;
}
model_before[key] = value_ptr;    // tree now owns it; rb_destroy(t)'s value_free will free it
```

Note `free(value_ptr)` here is a **plain `free`**, not the counting destructor passed to
`rb_create` — the tree never owned this value, so routing it through `value_free` would
misreport the destructor-call-count used elsewhere to prove non-absorption, and would risk
being confused with a tree-driven free. Every other value in `model_before` is tree-owned
and is reclaimed exactly once, by `rb_destroy(t)`'s call to `value_free` at the end of the
iteration. This is what makes the sweep run clean under `make asan`/`make memcheck`: every
value is freed exactly once, either by the harness (rejected values) or by the tree
(absorbed values), never both, never neither.

## 8. Ordered work: harness first, seam change second (red → green)

Section 8's earlier draft listed the fault-triggering tests (old items 3-8) as coming
*before* the seam-linkage edit. That's impossible as written: while `src/rbtree.c:24-25`
still defines its own `static rb_malloc`/`rb_free`, `rb_insert`/`rb_create` call those
static copies — static (internal) linkage is resolved at compile time within `rbtree.c`'s
own translation unit, so linking `tests/fault_alloc.c`'s (separately, externally linked)
`rb_malloc`/`rb_free` alongside it builds fine (no duplicate-symbol error — the two
`rb_malloc`s have different linkage) but is **inert**: arming the injector cannot affect
what `rbtree.c` actually calls. Tests 3-8 would either hang waiting on an injection that
never comes or pass for the wrong reason. Corrected sequence, preserving tests-first:

**Phase A — build the harness, run it red against today's `rbtree.c` (no `rbtree.c` edits yet):**
1. `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` implementing exactly `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`,
   `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`, `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)` per
   section 7b, plus the `Makefile` edit (section 7a: both link lines + `-Itests`) adding it
   to both binaries' sources. At this point it links but is dead code — `rbtree.c`'s own
   `static` definitions still win inside `rbtree.c`.
2. Write tests 3-8 below against the still-unchanged `rbtree.c` and run them. **Expected
   result: red**, in one specific, recorded way — e.g. `fault_alloc_arm(1)` before
   `rb_create` does not make it return `NULL`, because `rb_create` never called the
   injector's `rb_malloc` at all (`fault_alloc_total()` stays `0`). Recording this exact
   red state is the point: it proves the harness fails *because the seam isn't wired*, not
   for some unrelated reason, before the fix ever touches `rbtree.c`.

**Phase B — the one seam-only change:**
3. Delete `src/rbtree.c:24-25`'s two `static` definitions; add `#include "fault_alloc.h"`
   (section 7a). No other line in `rbtree.c` changes — confirmed unnecessary by sections 1
   and 4 (no `rb_insert`/`rb_delete` logic change is implied by wiring the seam).

**Phase C — rerun the same tests, now green:**
4. Rerun tests 3-8 unmodified against the patched `rbtree.c`; they should now pass, proving
   the seam change (and only the seam change) is what fixed them.

**The tests themselves (written once in Phase A, unchanged through Phase C):**

- **Test 3 (`rb_create` failure):** `fault_alloc_arm(1)` immediately before `rb_create`:
  assert `rb_create` returns `NULL` and `fault_alloc_total()==1`.
- **Test 4 (node-struct alloc failure):** `fault_alloc_arm(2)` with `rb_create` succeeding

## 9. Risks / assumptions

- Could not read `CS370-HW2.pdf` directly in this environment (no poppler-utils) to
  confirm Mutation 1's scope boundary in the spec's own words — this plan is built from
  CLAUDE.md + NOTES.md + the actual code, plus your corrections. Worth a manual cross-check

  have been framed as test-only work.
- One-induced-failure-per-iteration design doesn't test a *second* failure later in the

  pre-decided here; that gets designed when Mutation 2 actually requires it, against
  whatever this seam looks like at that point.

# Mutation 1 — allocation-failure fault injection: analysis & plan

## Context

HW2 requires every heap allocation in `src/rbtree.c` to be checked, with every failure
leaving the tree structurally and logically unchanged (same keys, same values, same
validated shape) with ownership unchanged — caller-owned values still caller-owned — and no
leaks (`make asan` / `make memcheck` clean). Today `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are `static`
pass-throughs to libc, and `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` are empty stubs. Mutation 1 is the
work that turns the seam into something a deterministic fault injector can sit underneath,
and proves `rb_insert` (the only non-trivial allocator in the file) is atomic against
injected failures. This plan is built from the actual current `src/rbtree.c` /
`include/rbtree.h` / `tests/test_rbtree.c` and from CLAUDE.md/NOTES.md — I could not read
`CS370-HW2.pdf` directly (no `pdftotext`/`poppler-utils` in this environment), so anything
here that assumes Mutation 1's scope boundary should be checked against the PDF's own
wording before final sign-off.

Interface (verbatim, per your spec): `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`, `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`,

- `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`: sets `fail_at = n` (n ≥ 1), resets `calls_since_arm = 0`, and

  observed since the most recent `fault_alloc_arm()` call, armed or not.

### 7b. `tests/fault_alloc.h` / `tests/fault_alloc.c` — exact semantics

Interface (verbatim, per your spec): `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`, `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`,
`fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)`.

Internal state: one call counter (`long calls_since_arm`), one target (`long fail_at`, 0 =
disarmed/never-fail).

- `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`: sets `fail_at = n` (n ≥ 1), resets `calls_since_arm = 0`, and
  enables injection. This is the **only** place the counter resets.
- `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`: sets `fail_at = 0` (no call will ever be injected again).
  It does **not** reset `calls_since_arm` — the spec never promises disarm touches the
  counter, so the design doesn't rely on it doing anything beyond turning injection off.
- `fault_alloc_total(void)`: returns `calls_since_arm` — count of `rb_malloc` calls
  observed since the most recent `fault_alloc_arm()` call, armed or not.
- `rb_malloc(size_t n)`: `calls_since_arm++`; if armed and `calls_since_arm == fail_at`,
  return `NULL` without calling real `malloc`; otherwise forward to real `malloc`.
- `rb_free(void *p)`: always forwards to real `free`, unconditionally — never injected.

**Why "since-last-arm," not lifetime-total or since-last-disarm:** the sweep only ever
needs one fact per iteration — how many `rb_malloc` calls happened during *this* armed
run. `fault_alloc_arm(n)` resetting the counter makes `fault_alloc_total()` at any point
during or after that run answer exactly that, with no dependence on how many allocations
happened in prior iterations or on whether `disarm()` resets anything (which the spec
never specifies). This is sufficient for both checks the sweep needs:
1. When injection fires, `fault_alloc_total() == n` by construction (the counter hits
   `fail_at` at the moment of injection) — nothing more needs to be assumed.
2. When a full scenario replay finishes with no `-1` anywhere, `fault_alloc_total()` at
   that point is the *true total allocations the scenario makes*, which is `< n` by
   definition (if it were `≥ n` injection would already have fired) — this is exactly the
   "run completed without hitting the fault" signal the termination rule needs, with no
   separate lifetime counter required.

### 7c. Deterministic fixed scenario

A small, hand-picked, non-random sequence of `rb_insert` calls, reused identically every
iteration, chosen to trigger at least one rotation/recolor in `insert_fixup` — so the sweep
also demonstrates failures never reach fixup (section 3), not merely that the two
`if`-checks exist. No randomness: every iteration's failing call must be exactly
reproducible and nameable in a failure report.

### 7d. Sweep loop and termination

```
n = 1
loop:
    fault_alloc_arm(n)
    t = rb_create(counting_free)
    if (t == NULL):
        assert fault_alloc_total() == n       # rb_create's own malloc was call n
        fault_alloc_disarm()                  # every iteration ends disarmed, including this branch
        n++; continue

    model_before = {}                          # key -> value, built as scenario replays
    observed_failure = false
    for (key, value) in fixed_scenario:
        size_before  = rb_size(t)
        find_before  = rb_find(t, key)          # section 7e, requirement 3
        rc = rb_insert(t, key, value)
        if (rc == -1):
            assert fault_alloc_total() == n
            assert_unchanged(t, model_before, key, find_before, size_before, value)
            observed_failure = true
            break
        model_before[key] = value               # only on success

    total = fault_alloc_total()                 # read before disarm (disarm doesn't touch it anyway)
    assert rb_validate(t) == 0                   # checked on every run, including the successful
                                                  # terminating one, before the tree is torn down
    rb_destroy(t)
    fault_alloc_disarm()

    if (total < n):
        # allocation n was never reached by anything in the scenario -- the legitimate
        # termination condition, per the spec's "until a run completes without hitting
        # the fault." This must coincide with observed_failure == false; if the scenario
        # ran dry (total < n) yet we somehow saw an rc == -1 earlier, that is itself a bug
        # to report (a -1 return not explained by any injected allocation failure).
        assert !observed_failure
        break                                   # sweep done
    else:
        # total >= n: the injected allocation WAS reached. The corresponding call is
        # REQUIRED to have returned its documented error code -- if observed_failure is
        # still false here, some API call swallowed a NULL from rb_malloc and returned
        # success anyway. That is a correctness bug the harness must fail the test on,
        # not a reason to treat the sweep as finished.
        assert observed_failure
        n++
```

Note the earlier draft's `if (!hit) break` conflated two different things: "rc == -1 never
happened" was being read as "allocation n was never reached," but those only coincide when
the API under test is correct. Using `fault_alloc_total()` against `n` (not merely whether
`-1` was ever returned) is what actually distinguishes "legitimately finished" from "a
buggy call silently absorbed a failed allocation" — the latter must fail the test, not end
the sweep. This also still answers the `rb_create`-vs-`rb_insert` split (Q6) the same way:
a failure landing in `rb_create` has no tree/model yet, so only the `NULL` return and
`fault_alloc_total()==n` are checked; one landing in `rb_insert` has a live tree and a
partial model from prior successful inserts in this run, checked by `assert_unchanged`.

### 7e. `assert_unchanged` — tightened to the spec's five minimums

Given the model dict (keys successfully inserted so far in *this* run) and the pre-call
snapshot (`size_before`, `find_before` for the about-to-fail key):

1. `rb_validate(t) == 0`.
2. `rb_size(t) == size_before`.
3. `rb_find(t, failed_key) == find_before` (for a brand-new key this is `NULL` both times;
   for a failing overwrite it's the prior value, unchanged).
4. For every other key already in `model_before`: `rb_find(t, other_key) == model_before[other_key]`.
5. The counting destructor's call count (`free_count`, reusing the existing
   `tests/test_rbtree.c:69-94` pattern) is unchanged from immediately before the call —
   the caller-owned `value` passed to the failed `rb_insert` was never freed by the tree.

No full in-order snapshot/array capture is needed — `rb_find` against the model plus
`rb_size`/`rb_validate`/the destructor counter is the spec's exact minimum and is simpler
than the in-order-dump approach from the previous revision.

### 7f. Value ownership *inside the harness itself*

The harness must not leak the thing it's using to prove the tree doesn't leak. When
`rb_insert(t, key, value_ptr)` returns `-1`, the tree never absorbed `value_ptr` — ownership
stayed with the caller, i.e. with the harness. If `value_ptr` was heap-allocated (it must
be, so a counting/tagged destructor can tell absorbed from not), **the harness is now the
only thing that will ever free it**, since `rb_destroy(t)` only calls `value_free` on nodes
the tree actually holds.

Concretely, per sweep iteration (section 7d): the scenario's values are generated fresh
each iteration (a small factory called right before each `rb_insert`, not a shared array
reused across iterations — once one iteration's tree absorbs and later destroys a value,
that value is gone; it can't be reused by the next `n`). Exactly one value per iteration is
ever at risk: the one passed to the call that fails (the loop breaks on the first `-1`, so
at most one failed insert per iteration). Immediately after `assert_unchanged` confirms the
tree didn't touch it:

```
rc = rb_insert(t, key, value_ptr);
if (rc == -1) {
    assert_unchanged(...);        // includes: destructor call count unchanged
    assert(fault_alloc_total() == n);
    free(value_ptr);              // harness, as caller, reclaims what it still owns
    hit = true;
    break;
}
model_before[key] = value_ptr;    // tree now owns it; rb_destroy(t)'s value_free will free it
```

Note `free(value_ptr)` here is a **plain `free`**, not the counting destructor passed to
`rb_create` — the tree never owned this value, so routing it through `value_free` would
misreport the destructor-call-count used elsewhere to prove non-absorption, and would risk
being confused with a tree-driven free. Every other value in `model_before` is tree-owned
and is reclaimed exactly once, by `rb_destroy(t)`'s call to `value_free` at the end of the
iteration. This is what makes the sweep run clean under `make asan`/`make memcheck`: every
value is freed exactly once, either by the harness (rejected values) or by the tree
(absorbed values), never both, never neither.

## 8. Ordered work: harness first, seam change second (red → green)

**Phase B — the one seam-only change:**
3. Delete `src/rbtree.c:24-25`'s two `static` definitions; add `#include "fault_alloc.h"`

   and 4 (no `rb_insert`/`rb_delete` logic change is implied by wiring the seam).

**Phase C — rerun the same tests, now green:**
4. Rerun tests 3-8 unmodified against the patched `rbtree.c`; they should now pass, proving
   the seam change (and only the seam change) is what fixed them.

**The tests themselves (written once in Phase A, unchanged through Phase C):**

## Context

HW2 requires every heap allocation in `src/rbtree.c` to be checked, with every failure
leaving the tree structurally and logically unchanged (same keys, same values, same
validated shape) with ownership unchanged — caller-owned values still caller-owned — and no
leaks (`make asan` / `make memcheck` clean). Today `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` are `static`
pass-throughs to libc, and `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` are empty stubs. Mutation 1 is the
work that turns the seam into something a deterministic fault injector can sit underneath,
and proves `rb_insert` (the only non-trivial allocator in the file) is atomic against
injected failures. This plan is built from the actual current `src/rbtree.c` /
`include/rbtree.h` / `tests/test_rbtree.c` and from CLAUDE.md/NOTES.md — I could not read
`CS370-HW2.pdf` directly (no `pdftotext`/`poppler-utils` in this environment), so anything
here that assumes Mutation 1's scope boundary should be checked against the PDF's own
wording before final sign-off.

## 1. Every allocation reachable from `rb_insert`, in source order

`rb_insert` (`src/rbtree.c:120-158`):

| # | Line | Allocation | Owner immediately after success | On failure | Resource(s) to release |
|---|------|------------|----------------------------------|------------|-------------------------|
| — | 126-129 (overwrite, `cmp==0`) | **none** | n/a | n/a (cannot fail) | n/a |
| 1 | 135 `n = rb_malloc(sizeof *n)` | new node struct | local `n` (not yet linked into the tree) | `return -1` immediately (136) | nothing — this was the only thing acquired, and it never succeeded |
| 2 | 139 `n->key = rb_malloc(keylen)` | key copy | local `n->key` (still not linked into the tree) | `rb_free(n); return -1;` (140-142) | `n` (the node struct from #1) |

No other `rb_malloc` call exists anywhere in `rb_insert`. `rb_create` (line 30-37) has
exactly one more allocation in the whole file (the `rbtree_t` struct itself), fails with
`return NULL` before any state exists, and already needs no unwind.

## 2. Candidate commit point

Line 151-153:
```c
if (parent == NULL)      t->root = n;
else if (cmp < 0)        parent->left = n;
else                     parent->right = n;
```
This is the **first** line that mutates the tree itself (first write to `t->root` or to an
existing node's `left`/`right`). Everything before it — both `rb_malloc` calls, `memcpy`,
and populating `n`'s fields — touches only the new, not-yet-linked node.

Both allocation failure points (#1 and #2 above) occur **strictly before** line 151 — by
construction, since both `rb_malloc` calls happen textually earlier and nothing branches
back. Consequence: **`insert_fixup` can never run on a failed `rb_insert`** — it is only
called (line 155) after the unconditional link-in, so there is no fixup-reachable fault
path to worry about at all for Mutation 1. There are no failure points after the commit
point in the current code, and none should be introduced.

**No new structure is needed.** The acquire-everything-before-mutating-anything ordering
already gives failure atomicity for free: at every failure point there is at most one
resource to release (none for #1, just `n` for #2), and the existing plain
`if (... == NULL) { cleanup; return -1; }` pairs already do that, LIFO, with no reordering
required. Per CLAUDE.md ("do not add cleanup paths that can instead be designed away") and
the house goto-cleanup rule (reserved for *multi-step* unwinds), introducing a
`goto cleanup` label here would be unneeded ceremony for a single-step release — recommend
leaving this exactly as-is. Flagging this as a judgment call since you said you'd push

allocations regardless of unwind complexity, that's a style call to settle explicitly.

- `rb_free(void *p)`: always forwards to real `free`, unconditionally — never injected.

**Why "since-last-arm," not lifetime-total or since-last-disarm:** the sweep only ever
needs one fact per iteration — how many `rb_malloc` calls happened during *this* armed
run. `fault_alloc_arm(n)` resetting the counter makes `fault_alloc_total()` at any point
during or after that run answer exactly that, with no dependence on how many allocations
happened in prior iterations or on whether `disarm()` resets anything (which the spec
never specifies). This is sufficient for both checks the sweep needs:
1. When injection fires, `fault_alloc_total() == n` by construction (the counter hits
   `fail_at` at the moment of injection) — nothing more needs to be assumed.
2. When a full scenario replay finishes with no `-1` anywhere, `fault_alloc_total()` at
   that point is the *true total allocations the scenario makes*, which is `< n` by
   definition (if it were `≥ n` injection would already have fired) — this is exactly the
   "run completed without hitting the fault" signal the termination rule needs, with no
   separate lifetime counter required.

### 7c. Deterministic fixed scenario

A small, hand-picked, non-random sequence of `rb_insert` calls, reused identically every
iteration, chosen to trigger at least one rotation/recolor in `insert_fixup` — so the sweep
also demonstrates failures never reach fixup (section 3), not merely that the two
`if`-checks exist. No randomness: every iteration's failing call must be exactly
reproducible and nameable in a failure report.

### 7d. Sweep loop and termination

```
n = 1
loop:
    fault_alloc_arm(n)
    t = rb_create(counting_free)
    if (t == NULL):
        assert fault_alloc_total() == n       # rb_create's own malloc was call n
        fault_alloc_disarm()                  # every iteration ends disarmed, including this branch
        n++; continue

    model_before = {}                          # key -> value, built as scenario replays
    observed_failure = false
    for (key, value) in fixed_scenario:
        size_before  = rb_size(t)
        find_before  = rb_find(t, key)          # section 7e, requirement 3
        rc = rb_insert(t, key, value)
        if (rc == -1):
            assert fault_alloc_total() == n
            assert_unchanged(t, model_before, key, find_before, size_before, value)
            observed_failure = true
            break
        model_before[key] = value               # only on success

    total = fault_alloc_total()                 # read before disarm (disarm doesn't touch it anyway)
    assert rb_validate(t) == 0                   # checked on every run, including the successful
                                                  # terminating one, before the tree is torn down
    rb_destroy(t)
    fault_alloc_disarm()

    if (total < n):
        # allocation n was never reached by anything in the scenario -- the legitimate
        # termination condition, per the spec's "until a run completes without hitting
        # the fault." This must coincide with observed_failure == false; if the scenario
        # ran dry (total < n) yet we somehow saw an rc == -1 earlier, that is itself a bug
        # to report (a -1 return not explained by any injected allocation failure).
        assert !observed_failure
        break                                   # sweep done
    else:
        # total >= n: the injected allocation WAS reached. The corresponding call is
        # REQUIRED to have returned its documented error code -- if observed_failure is
        # still false here, some API call swallowed a NULL from rb_malloc and returned
        # success anyway. That is a correctness bug the harness must fail the test on,
        # not a reason to treat the sweep as finished.
        assert observed_failure
        n++
```

Note the earlier draft's `if (!hit) break` conflated two different things: "rc == -1 never
happened" was being read as "allocation n was never reached," but those only coincide when
the API under test is correct. Using `fault_alloc_total()` against `n` (not merely whether
`-1` was ever returned) is what actually distinguishes "legitimately finished" from "a
buggy call silently absorbed a failed allocation" — the latter must fail the test, not end
the sweep. This also still answers the `rb_create`-vs-`rb_insert` split (Q6) the same way:
a failure landing in `rb_create` has no tree/model yet, so only the `NULL` return and
`fault_alloc_total()==n` are checked; one landing in `rb_insert` has a live tree and a
partial model from prior successful inserts in this run, checked by `assert_unchanged`.

### 7e. `assert_unchanged` — tightened to the spec's five minimums

Given the model dict (keys successfully inserted so far in *this* run) and the pre-call
snapshot (`size_before`, `find_before` for the about-to-fail key):

1. `rb_validate(t) == 0`.
2. `rb_size(t) == size_before`.
3. `rb_find(t, failed_key) == find_before` (for a brand-new key this is `NULL` both times;
   for a failing overwrite it's the prior value, unchanged).
4. For every other key already in `model_before`: `rb_find(t, other_key) == model_before[other_key]`.
5. The counting destructor's call count (`free_count`, reusing the existing
   `tests/test_rbtree.c:69-94` pattern) is unchanged from immediately before the call —
   the caller-owned `value` passed to the failed `rb_insert` was never freed by the tree.

No full in-order snapshot/array capture is needed — `rb_find` against the model plus
`rb_size`/`rb_validate`/the destructor counter is the spec's exact minimum and is simpler
than the in-order-dump approach from the previous revision.

### 7f. Value ownership *inside the harness itself*

The harness must not leak the thing it's using to prove the tree doesn't leak. When
`rb_insert(t, key, value_ptr)` returns `-1`, the tree never absorbed `value_ptr` — ownership
stayed with the caller, i.e. with the harness. If `value_ptr` was heap-allocated (it must
be, so a counting/tagged destructor can tell absorbed from not), **the harness is now the
only thing that will ever free it**, since `rb_destroy(t)` only calls `value_free` on nodes
the tree actually holds.

Concretely, per sweep iteration (section 7d): the scenario's values are generated fresh
each iteration (a small factory called right before each `rb_insert`, not a shared array
reused across iterations — once one iteration's tree absorbs and later destroys a value,
that value is gone; it can't be reused by the next `n`). Exactly one value per iteration is
ever at risk: the one passed to the call that fails (the loop breaks on the first `-1`, so
at most one failed insert per iteration). Immediately after `assert_unchanged` confirms the
tree didn't touch it:

```
rc = rb_insert(t, key, value_ptr);
if (rc == -1) {
    assert_unchanged(...);        // includes: destructor call count unchanged
    assert(fault_alloc_total() == n);
    free(value_ptr);              // harness, as caller, reclaims what it still owns
    hit = true;
    break;
}
model_before[key] = value_ptr;    // tree now owns it; rb_destroy(t)'s value_free will free it
```

Note `free(value_ptr)` here is a **plain `free`**, not the counting destructor passed to
`rb_create` — the tree never owned this value, so routing it through `value_free` would
misreport the destructor-call-count used elsewhere to prove non-absorption, and would risk
being confused with a tree-driven free. Every other value in `model_before` is tree-owned
and is reclaimed exactly once, by `rb_destroy(t)`'s call to `value_free` at the end of the
iteration. This is what makes the sweep run clean under `make asan`/`make memcheck`: every
value is freed exactly once, either by the harness (rejected values) or by the tree
(absorbed values), never both, never neither.

## 8. Ordered work: harness first, seam change second (red → green)

Section 8's earlier draft listed the fault-triggering tests (old items 3-8) as coming
*before* the seam-linkage edit. That's impossible as written: while `src/rbtree.c:24-25`
still defines its own `static rb_malloc`/`rb_free`, `rb_insert`/`rb_create` call those
static copies — static (internal) linkage is resolved at compile time within `rbtree.c`'s
own translation unit, so linking `tests/fault_alloc.c`'s (separately, externally linked)
`rb_malloc`/`rb_free` alongside it builds fine (no duplicate-symbol error — the two
`rb_malloc`s have different linkage) but is **inert**: arming the injector cannot affect
what `rbtree.c` actually calls. Tests 3-8 would either hang waiting on an injection that
never comes or pass for the wrong reason. Corrected sequence, preserving tests-first:

**Phase A — build the harness, run it red against today's `rbtree.c` (no `rbtree.c` edits yet):**
1. `tests/fault_alloc.{c,h}` implementing exactly `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`,
   `fault_alloc_arm(long n)`, `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)` per
   section 7b, plus the `Makefile` edit (section 7a: both link lines + `-Itests`) adding it
   to both binaries' sources. At this point it links but is dead code — `rbtree.c`'s own
   `static` definitions still win inside `rbtree.c`.
2. Write tests 3-8 below against the still-unchanged `rbtree.c` and run them. **Expected
   result: red**, in one specific, recorded way — e.g. `fault_alloc_arm(1)` before
   `rb_create` does not make it return `NULL`, because `rb_create` never called the
   injector's `rb_malloc` at all (`fault_alloc_total()` stays `0`). Recording this exact
   red state is the point: it proves the harness fails *because the seam isn't wired*, not
   for some unrelated reason, before the fix ever touches `rbtree.c`.

**Phase B — the one seam-only change:**
3. Delete `src/rbtree.c:24-25`'s two `static` definitions; add `#include "fault_alloc.h"`
   (section 7a). No other line in `rbtree.c` changes — confirmed unnecessary by sections 1
   and 4 (no `rb_insert`/`rb_delete` logic change is implied by wiring the seam).

**Phase C — rerun the same tests, now green:**
4. Rerun tests 3-8 unmodified against the patched `rbtree.c`; they should now pass, proving
   the seam change (and only the seam change) is what fixed them.

**The tests themselves (written once in Phase A, unchanged through Phase C):**

- **Test 3 (`rb_create` failure):** `fault_alloc_arm(1)` immediately before `rb_create`:
  assert `rb_create` returns `NULL` and `fault_alloc_total()==1`.
- **Test 4 (node-struct alloc failure):** `fault_alloc_arm(2)` with `rb_create` succeeding
  (its 1 alloc) and the fixed scenario's first `rb_insert` node-struct alloc as call 2:
  assert `-1`, full `assert_unchanged` (section 7e), harness frees the rejected value per
  section 7f.
- **Test 5 (key-copy alloc failure):** `fault_alloc_arm(3)` landing on that same insert's
  key-copy alloc: same assertions — tests 4 and 5 should be externally indistinguishable
  except for which internal `rb_malloc` call failed.
- **Test 6 (overwrite allocates nothing):** `fault_alloc_arm(1)` on a tree that already has
  the key, then overwrite it — must **succeed**, and assert `fault_alloc_total() == 0`
  afterward (strengthened: not just "didn't fail," but proves `rb_malloc` was never called
  at all, per section 5).
- **Test 7 (`rb_delete` allocates nothing):** `fault_alloc_arm(1)` on an existing tree, call
  `rb_delete`: must return `0`, and assert `fault_alloc_total() == 0` afterward (same
  strengthening, per section 6).
- **Test 8 (full sweep):** the loop in section 7d, run to its natural termination, under
  both `make asan` and `make memcheck` — this is what actually catches a harness-side leak
  of a rejected value (section 7f) as well as any tree-side leak.

## 9. Risks / assumptions

- Could not read `CS370-HW2.pdf` directly in this environment (no poppler-utils) to
  confirm Mutation 1's scope boundary in the spec's own words — this plan is built from
  CLAUDE.md + NOTES.md + the actual code, plus your corrections. Worth a manual cross-check
  before treating this as final.
- The `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` removal from `src/rbtree.c` (section 7a) is a real, if small,
  edit to `src/rbtree.c` itself, not purely test-side — flagging since "Mutation 1" might
  have been framed as test-only work.
- One-induced-failure-per-iteration design doesn't test a *second* failure later in the
  same tree's life after an earlier successful retry — likely out of scope per "every
  allocation may fail" being evaluated independently, but worth confirming against the
  spec rather than assuming.
- Mutation 2's slab allocator (`src/pool.c`) must use this same `rb_malloc`/`rb_free`
  seam — no additional build machinery (targets/macros/runtime dispatch) is being
  pre-decided here; that gets designed when Mutation 2 actually requires it, against
  whatever this seam looks like at that point.

- `tests/fault_alloc.h` / `tests/fault_alloc.c` (new content) — `rb_malloc`, `rb_free`, `fault_alloc_arm(long)`, `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)`, exactly per the approved semantics (since-last-arm counter, `fail_at==0` meaning disarmed).

No existing test was touched. `src/rbtree.c` and `include/rbtree.h` are untouched.

**Build:** clean, zero warnings under `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`.

**Run result — 10 failures, exactly as expected:**
```
FAIL: [rb_create] returns NULL when its own allocation is injected to fail
FAIL: [rb_create] fault_alloc_total is 1 at the injected failure
FAIL: [node-alloc] rb_insert returns -1 when the node-struct allocation is injected to fail
FAIL: [node-alloc] fault_alloc_total is 2 at the injected failure
FAIL: [node-alloc] rb_size unchanged after injected failure
FAIL: [node-alloc] rb_find(failed key) unchanged after injected failure
FAIL: [key-alloc] rb_insert returns -1 when the key-copy allocation is injected to fail
FAIL: [key-alloc] fault_alloc_total is 3 at the injected failure
FAIL: [key-alloc] rb_size unchanged after injected failure
FAIL: [key-alloc] rb_find(failed key) unchanged after injected failure
```
All pre-existing HW1 regression tests and the table-driven delete cases still pass; `build/fuzz 100000` still exits 0 (fuzz never touches the injector). `make test` stops after `test_rbtree`'s nonzero exit, as expected via the `&&`.

**Why this exact failure proves "linked but not wired":** `src/rbtree.c:24-25` still defines its own `static rb_malloc`/`rb_free`, so `rb_create`/`rb_insert` call those — never `fault_alloc.c`'s versions. Arming the injector before `rb_create` or an insert has no effect on what actually runs, so `rb_create` and the first `rb_insert` always succeed regardless of `n`, and `fault_alloc_total()` never leaves `0`. That's exactly the pattern in the output: `rb_create` returns non-NULL instead of `NULL`, `rb_insert` returns `0` instead of `-1`, and every `fault_alloc_total() == n` check fails because the counter never moved. That's expected per the plan and is called out in a comment at the top of the new test block; they'll only become meaningful once Phase B wires the seam.

Stopping here — no Phase B, no commit, no changes to `src/rbtree.c` or `include/rbtree.h`.

# PROMPTLOG

Trimmed to the 5 most substantive annotated episodes from a longer working log kept across the
`rb_delete` (M2) milestone, its coverage-audit follow-up, an adversarial review session, and the
session that closed the gap that review found. Each entry is: what I asked, what came back, and
my judgment call — accepted, revised, or rejected, and why. Corresponding commits: `71b55ac`,
`f32e9ef`, `8fa9072`, `ddfdbf9`, `ff09cbb`, `7a6e2b7`.

---

## 1. Plan revised twice under direct interrogation — imprecise control-flow claims caught before any test was written

**Prompt:** Asked Claude to plan a coverage audit of `delete_fixup` (M2 already landed the fixup
itself in commits `f32e9ef` and `8fa9072` — the loop, all cases plus mirrors, on 2026-09-13;
tonight's task was closing the gap NOTES.md already names: none of the 9
table-driven cases pin Case 4 (sibling black, red nephew) or Case 3 (sibling black, both nephews
black) in isolation, or a multi-level Case 3b climb / climb-to-root). Claude proposed a 5-slice
plan mapping each spec case to code and tests. Before approving, pushed on four specific claims
in that plan rather than accepting the slice boundaries as given.

**What came back, and what was wrong:**
- Claude's Slice 1 writeup said the Case-5 (red sibling) rotation causes the fixup "loop to
  re-enter." Asked for the actual control flow. Claude traced it and admitted the phrasing was
  imprecise: there is no `continue` or jump back to `while` after the Case-5 rotation — execution
  falls through, in the *same* iteration, into the Case-3/4 check now evaluated against the new
  (guaranteed-black) sibling. The loop only actually re-enters if that fall-through lands in
  Case 3b (parent black, debt climbs) and sets `x = parent`.
- Claude's Slice 2 lumped "sibling black, red nephew" into one case ("Case 4, terminal"). Asked
  whether near-red/far-black and far-red-directly are actually the same code path. They aren't:
  `rbtree.c`'s `else` branch has an inner `if (is_black(sib->right))` that only fires (and only
  then executes `rotate_right(t, sib)` to convert near-red into far-red) when the far nephew is
  black; the far-red-direct case skips that block entirely. Two distinct paths through the same
  branch, not one — Claude agreed and split Slice 2 into four sub-cases (2a/2b far-red-direct +
  mirror, 2c/2d near-red-conversion + mirror) instead of two.
- Asked why the plan asserted "no changes needed" for slices that already had passing tests, when
  passing tests (plus 10^5-op fuzz + asan/memcheck) aren't the same claim as "this specific named
  branch is deterministically pinned." Claude conceded the phrasing overclaimed and restated the
  actual scope: the algorithm's correctness evidence is the existing fuzz/asan/memcheck record,
  but the fuzzer's *aggregate* pass doesn't identify which named branch fired on any given op, so a
  regression isolated to one branch (e.g. the `rotate_right(t, sib)` conversion in Case 4)
  could hide behind an otherwise-green fuzz run for a while. Tonight's work makes that
  explicit and per-case, not a claim that the algorithm was newly proven correct.
- Asked, for Case 3a specifically, to point at the exact line where the red parent gets painted
  black — is it inside the both-nephews-black branch, or elsewhere? Claude traced it: the
  both-nephews-black branch (`rbtree.c:198-201`) only recolors the sibling and reassigns
  `x = parent; parent = x->parent`. The actual recolor happens because the *next* `while`
  condition check finds `is_black(x)` false (x is the old red parent), so the loop exits, and the
  post-loop catch-all `if (x != NULL) x->color = BLACK;` (`rbtree.c:243`) is what paints it black
  — not an explicit `if (is_red(parent))` inside Case 3 itself.

**Judgment: plan revised, not rejected outright.** All four corrections were accepted and folded
into the plan before any test code was written — this is the "one plan you revised" episode for
M2's audit work. None of the four changed the verdict that `delete_fixup`'s algorithm itself is
unchanged (it was committed 2026-09-13, before this session); what changed was the plan's
*description* of that algorithm's control flow and the honesty of its "verified" claims. Working
agreement going forward: derive and hand-verify one slice's tree/insertion-sequence at a time,
walk through why it actually enters the named case (mirror included) before writing any test
code, and don't pre-derive later slices — the same mistake that burned a turn earlier in M2, when
hand-simulated fixup colors for a "red sibling" test case turned out to disagree with the
compiled implementation once actually traced. This time it was caught before a fixture was even
...
262 PROMPTLOG.md

## 6. Mutation 1 plan — five rounds of pushback before a line of code was written, plus one post-implementation correction

**Prompt:** Asked Claude (in plan mode) to design Mutation 1: wire `src/rbtree.c`'s allocation
seam so `tests/fault_alloc.c` can deterministically inject allocation failures, trace every
allocation `rb_insert` can hit, and design a fault-sweep harness proving `rb_insert`/`rb_delete`
stay atomic and leak-free under every possible injected failure. Treated the plan itself as the
thing to interrogate before any file was touched — five separate rounds of correction below, all
during planning.

**Round 1 — invented interface, unneeded build scaffolding.** Claude's first draft invented its
own fault-injector function names (`fault_alloc_reset()` / `fault_alloc_set_fail_at()`) instead of
asking what the actual required interface was, and proposed gating `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` behind a
new `RBTREE_FAULT_ALLOC` macro with a second, separate "fault-sweep binary." Told Claude the exact
required interface (`fault_alloc_arm(long)`, `fault_alloc_disarm(void)`, `fault_alloc_total(void)`)
and pointed out the supplied Makefile already has exactly two binaries, both of which should link
the injector — no macro or third binary needed. Claude re-read the actual (not assumed) Makefile
and `fault_alloc.{c,h}` and reduced the design to: one seam, always linked, inert while disarmed.

**Round 2 — fault_alloc_total semantics and ownership tracing.** Asked Claude to justify exactly
what `fault_alloc_total()` counts (lifetime? since-arm? since-disarm?) against only what the spec
actually promises, and separately to trace who frees a caller-owned value when an injected
`rb_insert` failure correctly leaves ownership with the caller — a real leak risk in the harness
itself, not in `rbtree.c`. Claude settled on "calls since the most recent `fault_alloc_arm()`"
(justified by what the sweep actually needs, not by assumption) and added an explicit rule: the
harness frees a rejected value with plain `free()`, never through the counting destructor, so the
destructor-count assertion and the harness's own cleanup can't be confused with each other.

**Round 3 — a plan that looked tests-first wasn't.** Claude's task list put the fault-triggering
tests before the one necessary edit to `src/rbtree.c` (removing its `static rb_malloc`/`rb_free`
so the injector can actually intercept calls) — meaning those tests could not have passed yet,
making the ordering only cosmetically test-first. Caught this directly: "tests 3-8 cannot pass
before the seam change." Claude restructured into explicit phases — build the harness, run it red
against the unmodified `rbtree.c` and record *why* it's red, then make the seam-only edit, then
rerun the same tests expecting green.

**Round 4 — a termination-logic bug in the harness design itself, before implementation.** Claude's
sweep loop ended on `if (!hit) break`, where `hit` meant "some call returned -1." Pointed out this
conflates two different things: if a buggy API swallowed a `NULL` from `rb_malloc` and incorrectly
returned success anyway, `hit` would stay false and the harness would misreport the sweep as
legitimately finished instead of failing on the real bug. Claude reworked the loop to compare
`fault_alloc_total()` against `n` directly: `total < n` is the only legitimate termination signal,
and `total >= n` with no observed `-1` must fail the test rather than end the sweep.

**Round 5 (post-implementation) — an arbitrary safety cap that didn't belong.** After Phase A was
implemented and the expected red state confirmed, asked Claude to remove `FAULT_SWEEP_MAX_N` (a
64-iteration cap Claude had added as a belt-and-suspenders bound around the loop) since the
fixed, finite scenario already guarantees termination by construction — an unbounded `for (n = 1;
; n++)` relying solely on the `fault_alloc_total() < n` condition is both sufficient and closer to
what the spec actually says. Claude removed it in a 3-line diff and reran the focused tests,
confirming the same 10 expected failures, unchanged.

**Judgment: plan revised four times, implementation corrected once, nothing rejected outright.**
Every correction was caught before it reached committed code — four during planning (interface,
semantics, phase ordering, termination logic), one right after Phase A landed (the unneeded cap).
Pattern worth keeping: for fault-injection/property-style harnesses specifically, scrutinize the
*termination condition* and *ownership-on-failure* logic as hard as the production code being
tested — a bug in the harness's own loop can silently mask the exact defect (an API swallowing an
injected failure) the harness exists to catch.
